summary: A small green liverwort found from the Mediterranean region east to Turkey and along Atlantic Europe to north-western Scotland. Its flat body has a central rib, two wings and upright leaf-like ridges, and it grows chiefly in open, damp dune hollows.

Shrub native to North America, Central America, the Antilles and tropical South America. Its crushed leaves smell of garlic, and flowering occurs year-round toward the south but from spring through autumn toward the north.

An evergreen flowering vine native to tropical America, it has rough leaves and showy violet flower clusters. Depending on the climate, it may bloom twice a year, and its nectar-rich flowers attract butterflies.

A wetland biennial with hollow, often purplish stems and finely divided leaves, found beside rivers, estuaries and ditches. Its young parts contain a thin milky latex, and it is an important food plant for Old World swallowtail caterpillars.
edibilityNote: Roots have been used as a ginger substitute in southeastern Europe and Russia.

summary: A hornwort whose native origin is not stated, found worldwide in damp, shaded places. It forms flat, dark green rosettes on bare soil or rock and produces upright horn-like spore capsules. In temporary habitats it often grows annually, while tuber-like structures help it survive dry periods.
A perennial shrub native to the eastern United States, hoary mock orange can grow tall and bears white flowers.

Annual flowering grass native to Europe, Morocco and the Levant. It typically grows in coastal dunes and other sandy areas; in mainland Portugal, it occurs at only a few unstable dune sites along the northern coast and was assessed as Endangered in 2020.

summary: A perennial flowering plant native to the eastern United States, wild sweetwilliam forms upright clumps. It produces fragrant clusters of deep pink summer flowers on stiff, red-spotted stems.

A clumping palm native to tropical Africa, the Arabian Peninsula and Madagascar, with multiple stems and long, recurved green leaves armed with sharp basal spines. Its ripe orange fruit and palm heart are edible; in KwaZulu-Natal and Botswana’s Okavango Delta, sap tapped shortly before flowering is made into palm wine.
edibilityNote: Ripe fruit and palm heart are eaten; sap tapped before flowering makes palm wine in KwaZulu-Natal and Botswana’s Okavango Delta.

summary: Shrub or tree native to parts of Asia, from central and southern China to northern Vietnam, Taiwan, northern Sumatra and Mount Kinabalu on Borneo. It has closely clustered white flowers followed by small fruits and is grown as an ornamental plant.

An evergreen flowering shrub or tree found in mixed forests from China and Taiwan to Japan, the Philippines, Indonesia and India; its three recognized varieties are native to Taiwan. White spring flowers appear with red leaves and have a strong semen-like odor, while red fruits ripen in autumn and persist through winter.
edibilityNote: The leaves are toxic.

summary: A perennial flowering grass native to West Africa, tall reed is a fast-growing aquatic plant often found in swamps, along riverbanks and in standing water. Its young shoots can be cooked and eaten like bamboo or asparagus.
edibilityNote: Young shoots can be cooked and eaten like bamboo or asparagus.

summary: A herbaceous plant native to the Mascarene Islands and possibly also eastern Africa, other western Indian Ocean islands and the Arabian Peninsula. Its main stem bears scales rather than leaves, while secondary stems carry its leaves and tiny male and female flowers.

A running bamboo native to Zhejiang Province in China, yellow groove bamboo typically has dark green stems marked by a yellow groove, with occasional zigzag bends near the base. Its shoots are edible and lack an acrid taste even when raw.
edibilityNote: The shoots are eaten and are described as free of acrid flavour even when raw.

summary: A bamboo native to Hunan Province, China, it forms clumps of slender, arching canes that turn black after two or three seasons. Its plants flower together at long intervals and die after flowering.
edibilityNote: It is used as food in its native Chinese range and worldwide; the source does not specify the part or preparation.

summary: Flowering plant native to Europe and Asia. Its narrow leaves resemble an ox’s tongue, while its summer flowers are small, yellow and dandelion-like; it is invasive in Africa, Australia and North America.
A perennial evergreen herb native to the Caribbean, including Florida, and northern South America. Its creeping growth suits indoor hanging pots.

A herbaceous perennial whose native origin is not specified in the supplied information. It is widespread in central Europe and the Caucasus and naturalized in North America, with hollow, deeply grooved stems and white to pink flowers in rounded clusters.

A plant in the carrot family native to the British Isles, temperate Europe and Western Asia, burnet-saxifrage has leaves resembling those of burnet. It forms much of the turf on some southern English chalk downs and was formerly grown on lime-rich soils as livestock fodder.

A flowering tree native to the Pacific Coast and adjacent highlands of Mexico, Central America and northern South America, Madras thorn has a spiny trunk and fragrant greenish-white flowers. Its ripe pods turn pink and split open to reveal pink or white pulp, which is eaten raw in several countries and used in drinks.
edibilityNote: Sweet-and-sour pod pulp is eaten raw, served with meat dishes, or mixed with sugar and water for drinks.

summary: A rhizomatous plant native to Mexico and tropical America that grows in soil or on rocks. It occurs mainly in subtropical regions and has been widely introduced across Asia, Africa and Pacific islands.

A moss distributed almost worldwide, including from lowlands to the high Alps in Central Europe. It forms bright green, slightly glossy, flattened mats, often on tree bases or rotting wood, and produces reddish-yellow capsules whose spores mature in spring.
A small tree native to the West Indies and parts of Mexico and Central America, with glossy, blunt-tipped leaves. Its fragrant white flowers have yellow centres and grow in clusters.
An evergreen vining shrub native to South Africa. It has fragrant, bell-shaped pink flowers with darker markings and long capsules that release numerous winged seeds.
A moss with no stated native origin, urn hair moss is found across Europe, North America and parts of Asia. Its robust, upright growth may look bluish-green when moist, and its stems are wine red.

A leafy moss recorded across Europe, Asia, Africa, the Americas, Australia, New Zealand and Antarctica, it forms loose to moderately dense patches. Young growth is whitish to bluish-green, becoming reddish or brownish with age, while its capsules lean or hang from curved yellow-red stalks.

A perennial herb native to Europe, including European Russia, and Turkey. It has branching stems woody at the base and usually bears blue or violet flowers from May through July, with purple forms occurring rarely.

An evergreen shrub native to the paleotropics and neotropics, it has upright branches and variable, coarsely toothed leaves often edged in white or pale yellow. Small green flower clusters may be followed by black berries.

A tropical shrub or small tree native to eastern Malesia and the southwest Pacific islands, shield aralia has strong, bowl-shaped leaves historically used in Indonesia as dishes. Its shredded leaves can be mixed with meat or fish for their aroma.
edibilityNote: Shredded leaves are used in Indonesian cuisine with meat or fish; historically, whole leaves served as bowls rather than food.

summary: A widely distributed moss found across Europe, Asia, Africa, the Americas, Australia, New Zealand and Antarctica. It forms loose muddy-green, bluish-green or brownish growth, and its serrated leaves fit together when dry but bend back when wet.

A succulent annual flowering plant native to southern Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay. It has fleshy leaves and flowers in red, orange, pink, white or yellow. Unlike some related purslanes, it is described as inedible because of its bitter taste.
edibilityNote: The plant is described as inedible because of its bitter taste.

summary: Annual or short-lived perennial succulent native to the New World. Its unusually small, broad foliage accompanies flowers ranging from yellow and pink to orange.
edibilityNote: The stems, leaves, flowers and roots are all described as edible.

summary: A perennial aquatic plant of unspecified native origin, perfoliate pondweed is widely distributed across standing and flowing fresh waters on every continent except South America and Antarctica. Its translucent submerged leaves have no stalk and clasp the stem; it produces no floating leaves.

summary: A creeping perennial native across Europe, Asia and Africa. Its trailing stems root at their joints, while long stalks carry solitary yellow flowers with five heart-shaped petals, blooming from June to September in Europe.

A shrub or small tree native to China and long present in Japan, it is grown ornamentally and for cut flowers. Depending on the cultivar, its spring flowers are single or double and white or pink; its fruits are dark red.
A shrub or small tree originating from China, with pale pink or white flowers and red, softly hairy fruit. The widely grown Multiplex cultivar has double pink flowers.

A moss occurring especially in western, central and southern Europe, with further populations across several continents, it forms loose, fresh-green to pale-green patches. Its leaves curl inward and twist spirally when dry, and it favours sunny, often dry and warm ground rich in lime.
A vigorous bamboo native to Japan and Korea, it forms tall thickets with shiny, palm-like leaves and yellow-brown canes. Japanese samurai used its hard, stiff canes for arrows.

A rare herbaceous epiphytic fern ally from moist evergreen forests across parts of Asia, Australia, the Pacific and the Americas. It hangs from tree trunks and has repeatedly forked stems with minute scales but no true leaves or roots.

A rootless fern naturally found on all the main Hawaiian Islands, it also occurs widely across tropical and subtropical regions. Its leaves are greatly reduced, and it often grows on other plants in the tropics or in rock crevices in temperate areas.

A moss with no native origin stated, it has a circumboreal distribution. Its slender, nearly threadlike plants form flat yellow-green mats, commonly on deciduous-tree bark in Central European mountain forests.

sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A perennial fleabane native to Europe and western Asia, it grows in habitats ranging from semi-arid woodland to wet ground. It can spread by its roots into dense clusters and bears yellow flower heads that bend backward when setting seed.

Deciduous oak native to China, Korea, Japan, Indochina and the Himalayas; Flora of China also reports it from southeastern Tibet. Its leaves have numerous regular saw-like teeth, while its two-coloured acorns mature after about 18 months and sit in densely bristled caps.

Flowering tree endemic to Oklahoma and Texas in the southern Great Plains of the United States. It is often smaller and more likely to have several trunks than Shumard oak, with which it commonly forms hybrids between Dallas and San Antonio.

A moss with a circumpolar Northern Hemisphere distribution and isolated mountain populations farther south. It forms large cushiony mats on exposed, especially acidic rock, and its uniquely toothed leaf tips give it a downy appearance when dry.

A tiny annual herb native across temperate Europe, Macaronesia and parts of Africa and western Asia, allseed is easily overlooked. Its slender stems repeatedly fork, bearing minute white flowers followed by rounded capsules containing eight seeds each.

A perennial flowering herb native to northern North America, small yellow water-crowfoot is also present in Eurasia. It grows with creeping stems on moist ground or floating stems in shallow water, bearing divided round or kidney-shaped leaves and yellow flowers.

A small creeping annual or perennial plant of unspecified native origin, it carpets shallow water and muddy ground near ponds, ditches and streams. Its shiny, ivy-shaped leaves lack the finely divided submerged leaves of other water crowfoots, while its white flowers have yellow bases.
edibilityNote: Known to cause gastrointestinal distress; it was also sometimes used to treat skin conditions and wounds.

summary: A usually perennial flowering plant native to the broad Mediterranean region, although some varieties are annual. It is hairless and blue-green, with yellow flower heads whose outer petals have a pinkish stripe; its leaves are eaten raw or cooked, and its root is also edible.
edibilityNote: Leaves are eaten raw in salads or cooked; the root is also edible.

summary: An annual or perennial flowering plant occurring from Central and Southern Europe to Western Asia and North Africa; it is naturalized in Britain. Its stems branch at the base, and much of the upper stem may carry densely packed greenish-white flowers from April to September.

A moss of unspecified native origin, rose moss is found through most of the world in woods and sheltered grassy places. Its leaf rosettes resemble tiny green roses, and it mainly spreads through creeping stems that root at their joints; spore cases are rare.

A deciduous shrub native to the southern United States, orange azalea is especially associated with the Florida Panhandle region. Its abundant, pleasantly scented yellow or orange flowers appear in clusters before the new spring leaves and attract hummingbirds and butterflies.
Deciduous flowering shrub native to Japan, the Japanese azalea grows in grasslands and open scrub, never dense thickets or woodlands. It is also popularly cultivated as a bonsai.

A dwarf perennial shrub native to arctic and subarctic regions of North America, Europe and Asia. It can spread into long-lived colonies and bears evergreen leaves covered in golden or rust-coloured scales, with violet-pink to purple flowers that appear in spring and summer depending on latitude and elevation.

Flowering shrub or small tree native to eastern North America, staghorn sumac has rust-coloured, velvety stems and forked branches resembling antlers. Its foliage turns brilliant red, orange and yellow in autumn, while dense fruit clusters may remain from late summer through spring. The fruits can be prepared as a lemonade-like drink or jelly, and peeled shoots can be eaten raw.
edibilityNote: Fruits can be soaked, washed, strained and sweetened for a lemonade-like drink or used in jelly; peeled shoots can be eaten raw.

summary: A flowering tree native to North Carolina. Grown as an ornamental, it has pale pink flowers and flat seed pods.
A herbaceous flowering plant with no native origin stated. In Portugal, it grows along the margins of ditches and watercourses.
Invasive plant in the United States, likely introduced from Europe before 1818 in ballast water. It later spread through North America in contaminated nursery seed stock.

A perennial evergreen shrub native to southern China and Taiwan, Macartney rose often forms dense clumps and has recurved thorns and glossy, serrated leaves. Introduced to the United States as an ornamental, it has become invasive in some areas.
Deciduous shrub native to southern and central Europe, eastwards to Turkey and the Caucasus. It forms large patches and bears fragrant, deep-pink flowers, sometimes with doubled petals.
A shrub native to most of Europe, the Atlas Mountains, the Caucasus, Turkey, Lebanon and Syria. Its flowers can be pink, and its hips may remain after the leaves fall.

A shrub rose with reported wild origins from southern Iran to Afghanistan. Its white flowers have a musky scent from the stamens and bloom from late spring to late autumn in warm climates, but from late summer onward in cool-summer climates. Its small hips turn orange-red in autumn.
Rose native to central, southern and southeastern Europe, including southwestern Russia. Its fruit persists for about 30 days and contains about 23 seeds on average.

An annual grass native to the Mediterranean and Irano-Turanian regions. Its stems may stand upright or lie along the ground, and it bears a narrow, spike-like flower cluster; it commonly occupies disturbed ground, roadsides and fields.

summary: A woody-based perennial native to North America, primarily the south-central United States, with a disjunct population in northwest Georgia. It bears relatively large flower heads with yellow rays from late spring into summer.
A perennial herb whose native origin is not stated.

Perennial herb native across Europe and into the Caucasus and western and central Asia. It has large, broad leaves with crinkled edges. In mainland Portugal's 2016–2019 assessment, fewer than 100 mature plants were known from one population in the Montesinho mountains.

summary: Annual herb native to Canada and most of the contiguous United States. It has golden-yellow or greenish-yellow flower clusters on its leaves and stems, and narrow, wedge-shaped leaves. Its ground seeds are used in porridge, and its leaves are cooked as a vegetable.
edibilityNote: Seeds are ground into powder for porridge, and leaves are cooked as a vegetable.

summary: A herbaceous perennial flowering plant, it is eaten in spring as a leafy vegetable, pie filling and ingredient in broths and stuffed leaves in parts of Europe. Its leaves may be eaten raw or cooked but contain oxalic acid and should not be consumed excessively.
edibilityNote: Leaves are eaten raw or cooked, especially in spring, but contain oxalic acid and should not be consumed excessively.

summary: A perennial herb native to northern Europe and northern Asia. It grows in wet or disturbed places and has erect, often branching stems topped by dense whorls of green, pink or red flowers.

A perennial flowering plant found across most of Europe and not native to North America, wood dock favours damp, shady places, especially woodland. One variety has striking bright-red leaf veins, while another is entirely green. Its preferably young leaves are eaten, including in salads, but oxalates make large quantities inadvisable.
edibilityNote: Preferably young leaves are eaten raw in salads or as a wild vegetable, but harmful oxalates mean large quantities should be avoided.

summary: An evergreen fern native to South America, the Caribbean, southern Africa, western Indian Ocean islands, Papua New Guinea and Australasia. It forms bushy tufts of glossy dark green fronds, with round reproductive clusters beneath the leaflets, and its fronds are widely used in flower arrangements.

A palm tree native to far southern North America, Mexican palmetto has broad, fan-shaped fronds on spineless stalks and black fruit when ripe. Its decomposition-resistant wood is used for posts and pilings, while its leaves provide thatch and hat material.
edibilityNote: The ripe fruits and palm hearts are eaten.

summary: A perennial grass native across much of tropical and subtropical Asia, northern Australia, and eastern and northern Africa. It has spreading roots and has hybridized with domesticated sugarcane.
A shrub endemic to southern China, it has small green leaves, a woody, skin-like trunk and inconspicuous flowers. It produces small edible fruits, and its leaves have been used as a tea substitute.
edibilityNote: Its small drupes are edible, and the leaves have been used as a tea substitute.

summary: An evergreen perennial herb native to temperate Eurasia. It bears only a few flowers in the upper leaf axils, each with five sepals and five petals, and favors moist, nitrogen-rich ground, including coastal sands and peat.

A deciduous shrub or small tree native to Europe and western Asia, grey willow has green leaves with hairy undersides. In early spring, it bears male and female catkins on separate plants; male catkins turn from silver to yellow, while female catkins release tiny seeds in white down.
A willow shrub native to Europe and western Siberia. In northern parts of its range, it often develops into a tree.

A large shrub or small tree native to northern Europe and northern Asia, the laurel willow usually grows in wet or boggy ground. Its glossy dark-green leaves resemble bay laurel, and its spring catkins appear after the leaves.

Deciduous shrub or small tree native to Europe and western and central Asia, usually growing along waterways and in wetlands. Older bark flakes in large scales to reveal orange-brown patches, and male flowers unusually have three stamens.

A biennial or short-lived perennial native to southern Europe from Portugal to Bulgaria, with exceptionally soft, woolly leaves. They emerge silvery white, turn grey-green after flowering and become silvery again in cool autumn weather.

A herbaceous perennial native from southwest Texas through the Chihuahuan Desert to San Luis Potosí, Mexico. Its spicy-scented leaves accompany highly variable flowers, most commonly scarlet or red in the wild, and it blooms throughout summer and autumn.

An evergreen shrub found wild in southeastern Arizona and mountainous parts of Mexico. Its crushed leaves have a strong mint-like or blackcurrant-like fragrance, and its magenta, red, pink or rose flowers appear heavily in late spring and autumn.
edibilityNote: In central Mexico, the plant is grown medicinally and used to make tea.

summary: A short-lived herbaceous perennial reported as native to the northern Mediterranean Basin and parts of North Africa and Central Asia. It has thick, hairy square stems and pale flowers framed by large mauve, lilac, white or pink bracts.
edibilityNote: Historically added to wine and beer; its distilled essential oil flavors vermouth, wines and liqueurs.

summary: An annual floating aquatic fern native across parts of Africa, Asia and Europe, it grows in sunny, humid standing fresh water. Two leaves lie on the surface while a third stays submerged and functions like a root; air pockets in the leaves provide flotation.

A semi-aquatic perennial of unspecified native origin, widely distributed across parts of Europe, Africa, Asia, Australia and the Americas. It grows in wet places and bears small white flowers from spring to fall; its leaves were formerly agitated in water for use as laundry soap by local Arab people in Palestine.

A perennial plant widespread in shady European woodlands, wood sanicle has glossy, dark green, deeply lobed leaves. Its tight clusters of pinkish flowers produce bristly fruits that readily attach to clothing or animal fur.
A succulent native to Angola in Southern Africa. Its stiff, striped, nearly cylindrical leaves rise in a fan from a basal rosette, and its tubular greenish-white flowers are tinged pink.

summary: A carnivorous plant native to North America, it is now limited to a few sites in northern Alabama, North Carolina and Georgia, with historical records from Tennessee. Its tubular leaf traps contain digestive fluid and inward-pointing hairs, while older traps may flush pink or red.

A winter-annual herb found in Great Britain in dry, open habitats and on urban stonework, with no native origin stated. Its fleshy, three-lobed leaves, red stems and sepals are covered with numerous sticky glands.

A cosmopolitan moss. It commonly grows on calcareous stone and, in Central Europe, on walls, mortar and concrete; its stems are black-green and often nearly black when dry, with brown capsules almost hidden among the leaves.

A haploid moss found in China, Japan, Siberia, Europe and North America. In dim places, spherical cells concentrate faint light and create a green-gold gleam; it grows in shaded sites such as caves, animal-burrow entrances and upturned tree roots.

A freshwater club-rush of unstated native origin, widespread across Europe and much of Asia with a separate southern African population. It has round, mid- to dark-green stems, unlike the rounded-triangular stems of several related species, and most leaves are reduced to bladeless sheaths.
A perennial sedge of unspecified native origin, it has simple, broad leaves and a self-supporting form. It is associated with freshwater habitats.

A perennial herbaceous plant with no native origin stated, perennial knawel grows on sandy, dry, acidic soils. It has small white flowers and was formerly economically important as the main host of the Polish cochineal.

summary: A spiny herb native to the Mediterranean region and Canary Islands, with prickly wings running along its stems. Its divided leaves have white marginal veins, and yellow flower heads sit among spiny, leaflike bracts at the stem tips.

An annual or biennial herb with no species-wide native origin stated. It has divided leaves, yellow flowers sometimes reddish underneath, and brown fruits topped by feathery bristles; hooked flower-head bracts can catch on passing animals and disperse the seeds.

An annual flowering plant native from south-central and southeastern Europe to Iran and the Arabian Peninsula, Spanish stonecrop grows in loose, well-drained rocky soil. Its white flowers usually have six parts and petals marked by a purple midrib, appearing from March to June.
Flowering plant of unspecified native origin, known as Mexican stonecrop or Lemon Coral.

A succulent, evergreen perennial native to Europe and Asia. Its short, dense leaves form six characteristic spirals, and yellow star-shaped flowers appear in June and July, attracting bees and other insects.

A low evergreen vascular plant native to Macaronesia and parts of southern and eastern Africa, it belongs to the ancient clubmoss lineage rather than the ferns. It spreads through rooting stems to form dense mats of delicate, fern-like foliage.

A cactus native to the Antilles, Mexico and Central America, it climbs trees and rocks and has highly variable stems. Its large white flowers smell of vanilla and orange blossom, while the true species is extremely rare in cultivation and often confused with other species or hybrids.

An evergreen shrub native to Uruguay, southern Brazil, Paraguay and eastern Argentina, it inhabits wetlands, riverbanks and mountain edges. Its yellow flowers fold in shade and at night, while its fruit is a hanging cylindrical pod filled with seeds.

A foul-smelling shrub native to the southern United States, Mexico and South America, coffee senna has broad paired leaflets and yellow flowers in small groups. It flowers throughout the year and is an aggressive tropical weed.
edibilityNote: Leaves have long been eaten in Maldivian dishes, but sufficient intake may poison humans; seeds used as food in India have been linked to fatal childhood encephalopathy.

summary: A leguminous tree native to Maritime Southeast Asia and New Guinea, agati is fast-growing and soft-wooded, with rounded leaves and mildly fragrant white, red or pink flowers. Its long, thin green seed pods resemble beans.
edibilityNote: Flowers are eaten raw, blanched, fried or cooked; leaves are eaten young, and seed pods only when young.

summary: A flowering grass described as typically European and cultivated in many other regions as a food source. It has dense, hairy seed heads ranging from yellow to purple; cultivated forms retain their grains, unlike wild and invasive forms that shed them.
edibilityNote: Cultivated as a food source, with evidence of grain cultivation in prehistoric China and later Europe.

summary: Perennial grass native to temperate and tropical Asia. It spreads from a knotty underground stem and has broad, palm-like pleated leaves. In Papua New Guinea its cooked stem is eaten as a vegetable, while its grain can replace rice.
edibilityNote: In Papua New Guinea the stem is eaten after cooking, and the grain can be eaten as a rice substitute.

summary: Flowering undershrub believed to have originated in Central America and now found throughout the tropics. It has simple, coarsely toothed leaves and small clusters of yellow flowers; Indigenous people of Meghalaya’s Garo Hills use it to make brooms.
A self-supporting shrub with simple, broad leaves. Its flowers are visited by several bees, including the European wool carder bee.

Climbing plant native to Central America and northern South America, with large trumpet-shaped flowers and heavy, round fruits. Its green parts are highly toxic and have caused fatal poisoning; only the flesh of ripe fruit—not unripe fruit or seeds—is said to be edible.
edibilityNote: Only ripe fruit flesh is said to be edible; unripe fruit, seeds and green parts are toxic.

summary: A flowering shrub native to the southern United States, it has white stems and purple star-shaped flowers. Its leaves somewhat resemble those of a watermelon plant, and it is grown in home gardens as an ornamental.
A wild tomato species native to Ecuador and Peru. It produces small edible fruits and crosses freely with domestic tomatoes, making it valuable for introducing traits such as disease resistance.
edibilityNote: The small fruits are edible and were collected and eaten by the pre-Columbian Moche culture of northern coastal Peru.

summary: A perennial nightshade native to Peru and Ecuador. Its decorative fruits closely resemble cherry tomatoes in taste and texture but are mildly poisonous and may cause vomiting or gastroenteritis.
edibilityNote: The fruit is mildly poisonous and may cause vomiting or gastroenteritis despite resembling cherry tomatoes in taste and texture.

summary: A deciduous shrub native to temperate Asia, including Siberia, Russia’s Far East, northern China, Japan and Korea. Its fern-like toothed leaflets may redden before falling, while showy white flowers appear at branch tips in July and August.
An annual herb native to mainland Portugal. It grows chiefly on sandy soils in fallow fields and somewhat disturbed pastures.

A peat moss native to Europe, Macaronesia, the Americas, Asia and New Zealand. Pale green or olive plants have short, swollen side branches with blunt, boat-shaped tips, and favor constantly wet, fully lit, acidic, nutrient-poor places.

sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A moss with a cosmopolitan distribution.
A peat moss found across much of the world, prairie peatmoss mainly grows in wet forests and rarely in moors. It can absorb up to 30 times its dry weight in water and often forms large carpets.

Peat moss distributed mainly across continental-boreal parts of the Northern Hemisphere. It forms fairly large, pale-green plants with a prominent end bud and brittle stems; when dry, its branch leaves become wavy and curve backward like hooks.
Bridal-wreath is a garden plant native to Japan, Korea, China and Taiwan. It flowers in mid-spring, around May 5, and is sometimes cultivated elsewhere.

A flowering shrub native to east-central Europe and much of northern Asia, bridewort has been cultivated since the 1500s for hedges but can be unruly. It is also widely introduced elsewhere in Europe and eastern North America.
A flowering plant native to Asia, threelobe spirea has occasionally become naturalized in the United States.

A spreading perennial grass found across Australia, New Zealand, many Pacific islands, the Caribbean, Africa, India, China and Indonesia. It bears green or purple flowers and spreads through both above-ground and underground runners.

An annual herb native to Europe, western Asia and North Africa, field woundwort has branching square stems that may sprawl or stand upright. Its two-lipped flowers may be white, pink or purple and are arranged in clustered spikes.

A perennial flowering herb thought to be native to eastern North America, it is also widespread in central and western Europe and grows in wetland habitats. It has smooth, four-angled stems and white petals divided almost to their bases.

A yellow-green succulent shrub found worldwide; in New England, subspecies richii is native, while subspecies maritima is introduced. Its fleshy leaves turn red when they absorb too much salt. Young leaves can be eaten raw or cooked, though strongly salty, and seeds can also be eaten either way; protected populations may not be harvested.
edibilityNote: Young leaves and seeds are eaten raw or cooked; the leaves are strongly salty, and protected populations may not be harvested.

summary: A timber-producing plant native to South America, Mexico and Central America. It has very large leaves, while its upward-growing capsule fruits contain numerous winged seeds; its strong wood is used for furniture, musical instruments, ships and doors.

Flowering shrub native to North America, occurring from New Mexico through much of Mexico to Guatemala and Honduras. It is the tallest species in its genus, with pink, bell-shaped flowers and white or pale pink fruits.

A flowering plant native to eastern Canada and the eastern United States, New York aster grows in abandoned fields and wet meadows. Its cultivated varieties are valued for late-summer flowers in blue, pink and white.
Flowering plant native to Asia and introduced to Europe and North America, where it is sometimes a weed. Known as rough or prickly comfrey, it is the tallest species in its genus.
Large tree native to New South Wales and Queensland, Australia. It has deeply furrowed, fibrous brown bark and cream spring flowers fused into compound flowerheads.

A moss reported from Europe, western Asia and North America, it forms dense, cushion-like greyish mats. Its spoon-shaped leaves lie close when dry but stand upright when wet, and usually end in a long, toothed, translucent hair point.

An evergreen tropical tree native to the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia, it can live for more than a century. Its fruit changes from green through pink and crimson to black, has a sweet, mildly sour and astringent taste, and can stain the tongue purple; it is eaten raw or made into preserves and drinks.
edibilityNote: The fruit is eaten raw or made into sauces, jam, juice, jelly, sorbet, syrup or fruit salad.

summary: Evergreen shrub or small tree native to South Asia, Southeast Asia and China. It has shiny deep-green leaves and fragrant, waxy white pinwheel-shaped flowers, with both single- and double-flowered cultivated forms.

A winter annual grass native to southern and central Europe, North Africa and parts of Asia. Its drying awns twist and spread like Medusa’s snake-covered head, while tiny barbs help the seeds cling to animals, people and vehicles.

Shrubby marigold native to Sonora and Sinaloa in northwestern Mexico and southern Arizona in the United States. It blooms from fall into spring, sometimes for up to 10 months, and its foliage smells pungent when disturbed.

A succulent subshrub native to much of North and South America and the Caribbean, it has an unusually long orange root. It produces flower clusters and tiny jewel-like fruits, and can root again after being pulled if part of the root touches soil.
edibilityNote: The leaves are edible, and the plant is also reported to be consumed in salads.

summary: A deciduous conifer native to the southeastern United States. It mainly occupies still, nutrient-poor ponds and swamps, and has slender needle-like leaves held close to upright shoots. Its trunk is expanded at the base, even when young.
A flowering plant with no native origin stated. It is recorded from Ecuador’s coast and Andes.

An aquatic plant native to swamps, ponds and other wetlands of the southern and central United States. It has small violet flowers held above blue-green leaves dusted with white powder and edged in purple.

A perennial herb native to Europe, Northwest Africa, Yemen, Ethiopia, South Africa, Southwest Asia and Siberia. Its leaves are highly divided, and it grows in places including dunes, coastal rocks, chalky grassland, cliffs and rocky gullies.
A widespread moss found across North and South America from Alaska to Brazil, it is commonly known as delicate fern moss or common fern moss.

A perennial climbing plant native to western Africa, bush thunbergia develops densely branched stems that droop with age and may climb when supported. Its slightly fragrant flowers are usually velvety dark blue to deep purple with a yellow throat, though other colour forms occur.

A perennial climbing herb native to India, Thailand and the Indomalayan region, blue trumpet vine bears pale-blue trumpet-shaped flowers almost year-round. Each flower opens early in the morning and falls by evening, and the plant can become an invasive weed in tropical countries.
Erect annual flowering plant native to central and southern Europe, the Middle East, Central Asia, the western Himalayas and Xinjiang. It typically grows in steppes, disturbed ground and old fields.

A perennial herbaceous plant distributed across central and eastern Europe and Russia, Eurasian thyme grows in open dry meadows, grasslands and rocky places. In southern Banat, Serbia, its dried herb makes lemon-scented tea, while fresh leaves flavour homemade jams, candies and similar sweets.
edibilityNote: In southern Banat, dried herb is used for tea, and fresh leaves flavour homemade jams, candies and similar confections.

summary: A thyme species native to central, southern and western Europe, mother of thyme is cultivated as an evergreen groundcover. It has a strong oregano-like scent and can be used in cooking.
edibilityNote: It can be used in cuisine, though no plant part or preparation is specified.

summary: Small spreading flowering subshrub native to Europe. It has strongly aromatic leaves and lilac-pink flowers, with reddish square stems bearing hairs along the edges. It can be used like thyme in cooking.
edibilityNote: The plant can be used like thyme in cooking.

summary: Deciduous tree native to much of continental Europe and southwestern Great Britain, but only naturalised in Scotland and Ireland. It has broad, sharply toothed leaves, usually downy beneath, and fragrant yellowish-white flowers followed by woody, five-ridged fruits.

A flowering plant native to Mexico and Central America, perennial in its native habitat but grown as an annual in cooler climates. Its orange or red flower heads with golden centres provide nectar for monarch butterflies, hummingbirds and other pollinators.
An annual plant of unspecified native origin. It bears blue, white or pink flowers with yellow markings and has simple, toothed leaves arranged opposite or nearly opposite each other.
A flowering plant in the parsley family, native to mainland Portugal.

A moss occurring widely in Europe and also recorded in Asia, the Americas, North Africa and Australia. It forms dense yellow-green mats whose leaves curl and twist when dry, and its usually inclined spore capsules are produced only rarely.

An evergreen woody vine native to eastern and southeastern Asia, specifically Japan, Korea, southern China and Vietnam. It roots against wet surfaces or twines around supports, and cut stems release sticky white latex. Its leaves turn bronze in winter, while fragrant white flowers with twisted, pinwheel-like lobes appear from spring to early summer.

Trailing perennial herb native to the Gulf Coast of eastern Mexico, from Tamaulipas to Yucatan. Wild plants are washed-out grey-green-purple, while the commercially grown 'Purpurea' cultivar has purple-violet leaves and stems. Its three-petalled flowers open only in the morning.
edibilityNote: The leaves have been used as food colourants and preservatives.

summary: Herb native to Belize, Guatemala and southern Mexico. Its waxy leaves form dense rosettes, with dark or metallic green upper surfaces and glossy purple undersides. Small white flowers sit inside distinctive purple, boat-shaped bracts from spring to autumn.

A creeping perennial herb native to Mexico, Central America and Colombia, zebra spiderwort forms dense mats and is widely grown as a houseplant or warm-climate groundcover. Its leaves are striped silver and green above, with purple new growth and deep magenta undersides; prolonged intense sunlight can fade the stripes until the leaves turn purple.
edibilityNote: Its leaves are traditionally consumed as herbal teas or medicinal decoctions in parts of Latin America and Asia.

summary: An annual grass native to Europe, Asia and Africa. It forms clustered stems and grows mainly during hot, dry summer periods; Northern Hemisphere reports place flowering and fruiting in August and October.

A moss occurring across much of the Northern Hemisphere and into tropical Africa. It forms yellow-green to brownish-green mats, with leaves that curl when dry and spread upright or outward when moist; it rarely produces spore-bearing structures.

Annual herb native to Europe’s Atlantic coasts and the western Mediterranean, including North Africa, sea clover has unusually narrow, three-part leaves. After flowering, its calyx teeth curve outward, giving the fruiting heads a starry appearance.

Flowering perennial native to Eurasia and northern Africa. It is confined to salt marshes, estuaries and occasionally inland salt works, with purple flowers or rayless yellow forms. Young leaves are collected for food on floodplains in Zeeland, the Netherlands.
edibilityNote: Young leaves are collected for consumption on floodplains in Zeeland, the Netherlands.

summary: A perennial bunchgrass native to Europe, Asia and North Africa. Its flower clusters mature from greenish yellow or purple to bright golden yellow. The grass is toxic to livestock and can cause calcium deposits in soft tissues.

An annual wheat native from the eastern Mediterranean through Iran and Central Asia to Xinjiang, China. Its subspecies include durum wheat, used for pasta and semolina, and turanicum, usually milled into flour for bread and biscuits.
edibilityNote: Durum wheat is used for pasta and semolina; turanicum is usually milled into flour for bread and biscuits.

summary: A shrub thought to have reached Australia from China, Chinese bur is extensively naturalised across tropical regions. Its bark produces a type of jute, while its fruits bear smooth spines and its stems have star-shaped hairs.

A perennial subshrub or small shrub native to Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean, northern South America and southern Florida. Its bright yellow flowers open around sunrise and close or wilt by midday, while its mature capsules split to release seeds.

A large deciduous tree native across Europe from Ireland to the Urals and from the Arctic Circle to southern mountain regions, as well as the Caucasus and parts of Western Asia. Its tough, flexible young shoots lack the corky ridges found on many elms, while its rough leaves usually have an uneven base.

A leafy moss widespread across the Northern Hemisphere, with an additional occurrence in Tasmania. It forms rounded yellow-green cushions, and its leaves are strongly curled when dry but spread outward when moist. It usually grows on deciduous-tree bark, particularly in humid woodland.

summary: A vigorous perennial grass native to northern and central Africa and parts of the Middle East, para grass has creeping stems that root at their nodes, while detached pieces readily root in moist ground. It can form dense, invasive stands outside cultivation.
A deciduous shrub native to the southeastern United States. It has whitish-pink, bell-shaped flowers and dark blue berries with a pale waxy bloom.
edibilityNote: Berries are reported edible raw or cooked, although this claim is marked as needing a citation; harvest is mainly in late spring and summer.

summary: Flowering plant native to North America, Europe and Anatolia, typically found in lime-rich fens. Male and female flowers grow on separate plants and are pollinated by small flies; in Portugal it is recorded only in Minho beside small watercourses and in moisture-loving woodland and tall-herb communities.

summary: A flowering plant native to Europe and Asia Minor, orange mullein is a widespread weed in North America. It attracts pollinators and has been used medicinally for respiratory congestion and as a diuretic.

An annual flowering plant native to countries around the Mediterranean and slightly farther afield, pale speedwell has a sprawling habit and white flowers. Its leaves have five to nine lobes, and the plant may be lightly hairy, very hairy or hairless.
Herbaceous perennial; many varieties introduced to North America are native to Europe and Western Asia. It bears spikes of lilac-to-purple flowers and opposite, dark green, lance-shaped leaves.

An evergreen to semi-evergreen shrub or small tree native to the southeastern United States, it grows in woodlands, along streams and in moist hammocks. It has glossy oval leaves, white spring flowers and blue-black fruits eaten by birds and other wildlife.

A deciduous shrub native to mainland China, Korea, Japan and Taiwan. Its flat flower clusters have small fertile yellowish-white flowers in the centre, ringed by large showy sterile flowers; selected cultivars instead form snowball-like heads dominated by sterile blooms.
Annual herb native to the Mediterranean region and western and central Asia. Like other vetches, it climbs and bears feather-like leaves.

An annual climbing herb with compound, broad leaves. In mainland Portugal it is very sparsely distributed across the centre and south, growing around fences and the edges of dry-farmed fields and traditional olive groves on basic soils.

sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

summary: Shrub native to the Mediterranean region. It has aromatic foliage and midsummer spikes of lavender flowers, and several ancient Mediterranean cultures used it as a spice.
edibilityNote: Several ancient Mediterranean cultures used the shrub as a spice.

summary: An aromatic shrub or small tree native to tropical eastern and southern Africa and Asia. It usually has five lance-shaped leaflets, hairy beneath, and numerous white-to-blue flowers; its ripe fruit is black or purple.
A wild grape native to Texas, sweet mountain grape is notably drought-resistant. Growers have used this trait in hybrids and grafting.
A corm-growing plant native to South Africa. It is summer-dormant, grows during the winter rainy season, and has tall, fan-arranged strap-like leaves followed by spring flowers.

A deciduous shrub native to parts of northern and central China, the Russian Far East, the Korean Peninsula and Kyushu, Japan. It typically grows in scrub and mixed evergreen-deciduous forests and is attractive to hummingbirds.
A moss found widely on every continent except Antarctica, it forms green tufts usually less than one centimetre high. Each plant has both male and female reproductive structures.

Woody deciduous climber native to Japan. It produces exceptionally long clusters of fragrant white, pink, violet or blue flowers, while its clockwise-twining stems can extend across many supports. Its brown, velvety seed pods are poisonous.
edibilityNote: The brown, velvety, bean-like seed pods are poisonous.

summary: An evergreen fern occurring naturally in mainland Portugal only in the northern Gerês, Freita and Arestal ranges; the Sintra population is considered introduced. It has arching fronds with curved, finely toothed segments, and rooting plantlets can appear at their tips.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Woodwardia radicans
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

summary: An evergreen shrub native to the southeastern United States, especially coastal dunes and barrier islands. It has very stiff, narrow leaves with skin-piercing tips and tall clusters of bell-shaped white flowers, sometimes tinged purple or red.

A ground-hugging yucca native to northern Mexico and parts of the blackland prairies of northern and central Texas. Its nearly trunkless rosettes have pale blue-grey to sage-green leaves and produce tall clusters of light-green to cream, bell-shaped flowers.

A small, trunkless plant native to the Edwards Plateau of Texas and to Coahuila and Nuevo León in northeastern Mexico. It forms colonies of rosettes with distinctive twisted leaves and produces drooping white or greenish bell-shaped flowers from April through June.

A yucca native to Texas, Chihuahua and Coahuila, it has narrow, dagger-like, slightly blue-grey leaves. It can flower before developing a trunk, producing white flowers from late March to early May and dry, egg-shaped fruit.

Flowering shrub or small tree native to southern and central China, Taiwan and South Korea. Numerous short spines line its stems and leaf stalks, while rough reddish-brown berry shells split to reveal black seeds; it is one source of Sichuan pepper.
edibilityNote: This species is one of several used to produce Sichuan pepper.

summary: A bulb-forming rain lily native to parts of South America, with narrow, glossy green leaves. Its white flowers emerge from papery sheaths and can be tinged pink on their outer surfaces.
A perennial rain lily native to Peru and Colombia. It produces fragrant, bright pink flowers after heavy rains, while its bulbs contain toxic alkaloids that can cause vomiting, convulsions and death.
edibilityNote: The bulbs contain toxic alkaloids and can cause vomiting, convulsions and death in humans.

summary: A mat-forming perennial grass native to temperate coastal southeastern Asia and northern Australasia. It spreads vigorously to form extensive velvety green mats and grows well in sandy, salty coastal ground.
A moss with an almost cosmopolitan distribution.

sources.title: Zygodon viridissimus (Dicks.) Brid.
sources.attribution: Ros R M, Olaf S R, Eloy O W, Cerón E, plazi (2024). Revisiting the Bryophyte Checklist of Algeria: Exploring Diversity and Distribution. Cryptogamie, Bryologie. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/6xu7ry accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A giant water lily native to tropical South America, specifically Guyana and the Amazon Basin, it grows in still or slow-moving water. Its enormous floating pads have spiny undersides, while its flowers open around sunset and change from white to reddish pink during beetle pollination.

Evergreen forest tree native to Tasmania and Victoria, Australian mountain ash is the tallest flowering plant. It has a straight trunk with mostly smooth grey bark, rough brown bark at the base, glossy green leaves and white flowers.

A clump-forming flowering perennial native to southern Africa, specifically KwaZulu-Natal and Cape Province, society garlic has narrow leaves and fragrant violet flower clusters from midsummer to autumn. Its garlic-scented leaves are eaten as substitutes for chives or garlic, while Zulu people in South Africa eat the leaves and flowers like spinach or use them to season meat and potatoes.
edibilityNote: Leaves are eaten as chive or garlic substitutes; Zulu people in South Africa eat leaves and flowers as vegetables or seasoning.

summary: Evergreen shrub found on slopes, roadsides and beside streams in southern China, Japan, Laos, Cambodia, Thailand and Vietnam. It bears white or pink flowers, and its cooked fruit is edible and can be made into jam.
edibilityNote: The fruit is edible when cooked and can be made into jam.

summary: A flowering plant native from northern Mexico through Mesoamerica and South America to northern Argentina, it belongs to the sunflower family.

A begonia native to Central America. Its foliage has a distinctive notched and toothed shape. It is widely cultivated beyond its natural range, including in Peru, where examined specimens came from settlements and it does not appear widely naturalised.

sources.title: Begonia heracleifolia Cham. & Schltdl.
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A flowering plant endemic to the western Mediterranean, blue aphyllanthes has large, bright flowers and favors hot, dry, rocky habitats. A 2020 mainland Portugal assessment knew it only from the international Douro stretch, estimated about 275 plants nationally and classified it as Endangered.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Aphyllanthes monspeliensis
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

summary: A deciduous cherry tree native to Izu Ōshima and the Izu Peninsula on Honshū near Tokyo, Japan, the Oshima cherry is grown for its ornamental blossoms. In spring, it bears clusters of five-petalled white flowers with gold stamens, as well as small black cherries.
edibilityNote: Its fruit is edible; dried flowers make tea, and leaves are used in cooking, though P. speciosa is not the only sakura leaf used.

summary: Clustering palm native to Taiwan and Japan’s Ryukyu Islands. Its stems are wrapped in fine black fibres, while its fishtail-shaped leaves have silvery undersides. The fruit is reported to cause a severe allergic reaction.
edibilityNote: The fruit can cause a severe allergic reaction, but the exposure route and any edible preparation are not specified.

summary: Palm native to Minas Gerais and Goiás in Brazil. Its inward-arching, feather-like leaves crown a thick trunk, and its aromatic orange fruit is locally gathered from the wild for juice, marmalade, ice cream and liquor.
edibilityNote: Wild-harvested fruit is made into juice, liquor, marmalade and ice cream; oil can also be extracted from the nuts.

summary: A palm native to New Caledonia, where it occurs in humid and gallery forests. It is readily recognised by its glossy red young leaves, while its fruits turn red when ripe.

A flowering shrub of northern North America and Greenland, bog Labrador tea grows mainly in cold, acidic wetlands. Its evergreen leaves have leathery, wrinkled tops and densely hairy undersides, while its small white flowers form fragrant clusters. The leaves are brewed as tea, though concentrated doses may be toxic to humans.
edibilityNote: Leaves are traditionally brewed as fragrant tea; concentrated doses may be toxic to humans.

summary: A small annual fern found worldwide in temperate and subtropical regions. Unusually for a fern, one life stage tends to be annual, while another can remain dormant for up to two and a half years. Its delicate leaves bear long spore cases underneath their nearly circular leaflets.

An aromatic perennial native to tropical and subtropical Asia, Australia and the western Pacific. Its strongly scented green or purple leaves grow on a hairy, many-branched plant, with purplish flowers clustered in close whorls.
edibilityNote: Leaves are used in Thai stir-fries and curries and Minangkabau fish dishes; the plant is also widely consumed as herbal tea.

summary: An upright tree endemic to coastal and tableland New South Wales. It has deeply fissured dark bark, finely divided leaves, pale yellow or cream flower heads, and mostly straight, flat pods.
A biennial or perennial grass native to the western Mediterranean. It forms dense, carpet-like stands from long creeping rhizomes and has stiff, rolled leaves with often curved spikelets.

sources.title: Brachypodium phoenicoides (L.) Roem. & Schult.
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A corm-growing flowering plant native to southern Africa, especially South Africa, it produces three narrow leaves and a spike of large white or cream flowers marked with greenish or purplish lines. Some individuals have blooms scented like carnations and cloves, but others lack scent.
A flowering plant whose listed maritime and typical subspecies are native to mainland Portugal. Neither listed subspecies is protected by Portuguese or European legislation.
A perennial herb endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. It has a prominent basal leaf rosette and pale blue to violet flowers with five long, protruding reddish stamens.

sources.title: Echium lusitanicum L.
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: An annual squash native to the Americas, though its exact domestication center is unclear. Its fig-like leaves and oval, watermelon-like fruits stand out; the fruit, seeds, flowers, leaves and tender shoots are eaten, with immature fruit cooked as summer squash.
edibilityNote: Immature fruit is cooked as summer squash; mature fruit becomes sweets, drinks or pasta-like strands, while seeds, flowers, leaves and tender shoots are also eaten.

summary: An evergreen tree native to the Valdivian temperate forests of Chile and adjacent southern Argentina, maqui has flexible branches and leaves on strong red stalks. Its small purple-black berries are edible, taste like blackberries and are commercially gathered from wild plants.
edibilityNote: The small purple-black berries are edible, blackberry-like, and commercially marketed after being gathered mainly from wild plants.

summary: An upright evergreen flowering shrub typical of Mediterranean vegetation, Mediterranean spurge has narrow, densely hairy leaves and large clusters of yellow cup-like flowers. Its floral glands are dark in subspecies characias and yellow in subspecies wulfenii, and the plant tolerates prolonged drought and high salinity.

A bushy evergreen perennial native to southern Europe and southwestern Asia. It has somewhat fleshy leaves arranged in spirals and bears clusters of bright yellow flowers in late spring. Broken parts release a milky sap that can irritate skin.
edibilityNote: All parts are toxic if eaten.

summary: A plant in the pea family, with no native origin or other distinctive features supplied.

An evergreen shrub or small tree native to South Africa’s southern and southeastern coasts. Its mauve, pink, crimson or white sweet-pea-like flowers close at night and have a distinctive brush-like tuft.
A buttercup-family plant from the Azores, Madeira and Canary Islands, where it grows on moister sites. It has hairy, deeply lobed leaves and large, glossy yellow flowers.
A perennial shrub native to the Canary Islands. It bears loose groups of daisy-like flower heads, and its fragrant flowers open in the morning and close at night.

An evergreen shrub native to the western and central Mediterranean. It has arching, velvety white shoots, glossy aromatic leaves and pale blue summer flowers; the cultivar ‘Azureum’ has darker blue flowers.
A cool-season grass native to Macaronesia and the Mediterranean. Widely introduced elsewhere and invasive in some places, it can accumulate zinc and lead.

A large deciduous tree native from the eastern Mediterranean to Iran, though ancient cultivation makes the exact limits of its original range uncertain. It has a broad crown, flaking bark, deeply lobed leaves and hanging clusters of spherical fruiting heads. Its leaves may turn blood red, amber and yellow in autumn.

A climbing perennial native to South Africa’s Western and Eastern Cape, okie bean has stems that become woody at the base and pink-to-purple pea flowers. Its flat, curved pods explosively cast seeds, which can remain dormant in soil for some years.
Evergreen suckering shrub endemic to South Africa. Its blue-green leaves have a distinctive musky smell, and dark red, nectar-rich flower spikes appear in spring. All parts are poisonous.
edibilityNote: All parts of the plant are poisonous.

summary: A wild petunia native to Brazil, Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay. It has violet flowers and is generally smaller and harder to cultivate than the familiar hybrid bedding petunia.

Woody shrub endemic to eastern Australia, the knife-leaf wattle has crowded, leathery, triangular green-grey leaf-like structures. Its bright golden flowers appear from August to November in its natural range. The flowers are edible and used in some fritters.
edibilityNote: The flowers are edible and used as an ingredient in some fritters.

summary: Flowering plant native to the Canary Islands and Mediterranean shores. In Portugal it occurs in sometimes disturbed coastal habitats with some salinity, and it is used in research intended to improve sugar beet.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Beta macrocarpa
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

summary: An annual herb native to the western Mediterranean, it has an upright green stem and deeply divided leaves. Its flowers have four white petals, followed by long pods containing seeds in two parallel rows.

A dense rainforest tree native to New South Wales, Australia, with glossy green leaves and clustered white flowers. Its magenta, white, pink or purple fruit has a pleasantly sour, apple-like flavour and is eaten fresh or cooked into jam.
edibilityNote: The fruit is eaten fresh or cooked into jam and was historically fermented to make wine.

summary: Annual flowering plant native to Mexico. The wild plant has solitary heads with purple outer florets around black and yellow centres, while cultivated forms offer many colours, sizes and shapes. It flowers in summer and does not tolerate freezing temperatures.
A bushy shrub native to the Canary Islands and Madeira. It has large leaves, golden-yellow flowers and dry seed capsules that split open completely, and it can reproduce through rhizomes.

A woody climbing and sprawling vine native to North America. Its five-part, coarsely toothed leaves accompany small greenish flowers that become blue-black, oxalate-containing berries; unlike Virginia creeper, its tendrils lack adhesive discs and cannot climb smooth walls.

A small flowering tree of unstated native origin, occurring in southeastern Brazil, Paraguay and northeastern Argentina. Male and female flowers grow on separate plants, which have milky sap and glossy evergreen leaves with sharply toothed edges.

A prostrate perennial flowering plant found discontinuously in Western Europe and tropical Africa, Cornish moneywort grows in moist, shady places. Its thread-like stems creep, root and form mats beneath deeply notched, kidney-shaped hairy leaves; tiny pinkish flowers appear singly from June onwards.

An evergreen shrub native across the Middle East, North Africa and other African regions, southern Europe, the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia. It has dull green leaves, small green bell-shaped flowers and orange-red ripe fruit. Its root has centuries of traditional Indian medicinal use, but evidence remains insufficient to confirm the safety or effectiveness of marketed root or leaf supplements.

A rare tree endemic to Madeira and the Canary Islands, where it occurs in laurel forest. It has short branches, whitish flowers and capsules that become dark red when ripe; its heavy reddish wood was historically used for inlay.

A green alga found around Europe and on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts of North America. Its fine, hair-like filaments are unbranched; unattached forms create twisted masses, while attached forms grow in tufts from a base.

Red alga from the northern Atlantic and Pacific coasts, dulse has flat, branching, leathery blades that vary from deep rose to reddish purple. It attaches to rocks or kelp. Fresh dulse can be eaten directly, while sun-dried dulse is eaten whole or ground into flakes or powder.
edibilityNote: Fresh dulse is eaten directly; sun-dried dulse is eaten whole or ground, and it has been a dietary fibre source in Iceland for centuries.

summary: A marine red alga with a cosmopolitan distribution, rusty rock forms thin pinkish-red to reddish-brown crusts tightly attached to rocks and pebbles in intertidal and shallow subtidal waters. It tolerates a wide range of salinity, temperature and light conditions.
A small epiphytic seashore alga of unstated native origin. Its soft, hollow, dark reddish-brown branches are sparsely divided and twisted, and it generally grows on rocks in shore pools.

Red alga with no stated native origin, found on both sides of the northern Atlantic. It forms perennial tufts of wiry, irregularly branching reddish-black fronds attached to rock. It can be eaten raw or cooked and is described as crunchy and pleasant-tasting.
edibilityNote: Edible seaweed eaten raw or cooked; it was also used in the Soviet Union to produce agar.

summary: A perennial red alga widespread along Northern Hemisphere coasts; its native origin is not stated. It forms coarse, dark brown-red, heavily branched clumps and develops numerous pale red, brush-like branchlets in spring before becoming bare-looking again by summer.

sources.title: Rhodomela confervoides (Hudson) P.C.Silva
sources.attribution: Döring M (2022). German Wikipedia - Species Pages. Wikimedia Foundation. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/4wn9dt accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. It inhabits dry, exposed rocky places, especially granite and quartzite outcrops, slopes and crags.

A summer-deciduous shrub or small tree from the Mediterranean Basin, although its original homeland is uncertain because it is also an ancient introduction. Its bruised leaves smell like spoiled beans, and it remains leafy from autumn through spring before becoming dormant in summer. The plant is extremely poisonous, especially its bean-like seeds.
edibilityNote: All parts are very poisonous; the bean-like seeds have the highest toxin concentration and may be fatal if eaten.

summary: A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It occurs in scrub clearings, pastures, slopes and rocky ground, always on acidic or calcium-depleted substrates.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It grows in preferably sandy meadows that are temporarily waterlogged.

A small biennial herb endemic to Socotra, Persian violet naturally grows in rocky areas. It has dark green leaves and fragrant purple flowers with yellow centres, and cultivation has made it an occasional greenhouse weed elsewhere.

Perennial water lily native from northern India through China, Korea and Japan to Taiwan and far eastern Russia. Its large, round, puckered leaves, stems and spiny fruits bear sharp prickles, and its violet-and-white flowers often pierce the leaves. The seeds and leaf stalks are eaten; seeds are commonly dried and may be roasted or fried in northern and western India.
edibilityNote: Seeds and leaf stalks are eaten; seeds are dried and may be roasted, fried, made into porridge or pudding, or added to soup.

summary: A tree native to eastern Africa from Kenya south through Tanzania, Malawi and Zimbabwe to South Africa, it has a spreading canopy covered with large pink flowers in early summer. Oil from its seeds is used in African skin care, while the seeds are eaten by birds and monkeys.

Tree-like perennial cactus native from Brazil, Paraguay, Bolivia and Uruguay to eastern Peru and northeastern Argentina. It usually develops a single woody trunk, with cylindrical side branches and flattened, leaf-like terminal growth. Its lemon-yellow flowers open by day, while its fruit bears clusters of irritating brown bristles.

A small tree or large shrub growing in Victoria, Tasmania and New Zealand. It has straight, smooth-barked stems, leaves that are dark green above and pale grey beneath, and clusters of small, petal-free flowers. Only the coastal subspecies occurs in New Zealand, where fewer than 250 mature plants were reported.
Flowering tree native to South Africa, Eswatini and Lesotho. It has distinctive bottlebrush-like flower clusters and elliptical leaves.

A shrub or small tree native to South Africa, woolly bottlebrush has leaves with woolly undersides and bark that becomes grey and deeply furrowed with age. Dense upright clusters of scarlet flowers appear from July to October in its native range.

An evergreen shrub or small tree of unspecified native origin, it forms horizontally layered branches and has slightly rough leaves. Its abundant flower clusters are white to pale yellow or pink, while pink-flowered varieties may have green, copper, purple or red-toned foliage.

A small perennial shrub of unspecified native origin, it is recorded in France, Portugal, Spain, Morocco and Algeria. Its older stems develop peeling grey bark and often become gnarled and twisted, while violet to intense-blue flowers appear from March to May.

An evergreen tree endemic to a small area of South Africa’s Cape Peninsula, it has uncertainly native or possibly introduced outlying populations nearby. Its silky, densely haired leaves shine silver, and its woody cones contain seeds with parachute-like hairs.
A primrose-family plant found in the Macaronesian archipelagoes of Madeira and the Canary Islands. It is threatened by habitat loss.

A flowering tree native to Central and South America, from Panama to Brazil, the ant tree has smooth, mottled gray bark and showy pink flowers. Aggressive, venomous ants live inside the tree and defend it against intruders.

Succulent plant endemic to Madeira, where it is critically endangered and confined to one locality in Calheta. It has reddish-purple branches and bright golden-yellow flowers, usually with seven petals, and grows in sheltered rocky crevices.
A flowering plant native to KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, it is commonly known as Natal flame bush. It is the only species remaining in its genus after the others were transferred elsewhere.
Flowering plant endemic to central Portugal. It grows in rocky areas and on embankments in dry, exposed sites with acidic ground.

A flowering plant endemic to Madeira and restricted to its southern coast. The typical subspecies is known only from Pináculo, while subsp. coronopifolia is known from one population at Cabo Girão; both are Critically Endangered.

sources.title: Andryala crithmifolia Aiton
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A flowering plant endemic to the Madeira Archipelago. It is protected under Portuguese or European legislation and European wildlife agreements.

A flowering plant endemic to the north-western Iberian Peninsula, Antirrhinum lopesianum occurs in Portugal only in north-eastern Trás-os-Montes, on cliffs along the Douro and some tributaries. It grows on shaded, generally north-facing schist cliffs, sometimes among limestone outcrops or deposited carbonates.

summary: A perennial herb endemic to the limestone mountains of west-central mainland Portugal. It grows on rocky outcrops and stony limestone soils, producing white or pinkish-white flowers from March to June. Its habitat is declining locally because of wind-farm construction and quarry expansion.

A flowering shrub endemic to Portugal’s Berlengas archipelago, where it grows on rocky coastal cliffs and granite slopes. It bears small, pale-pink flowers in clusters at the ends of long stalks during April and May.

summary: A flowering plant endemic to mainland Portugal. It is protected under Portuguese or European law as a priority species under Annex II and is also listed under Annex IV of the Habitats Directive.

A bellflower-family plant endemic to the Azores, it bears pinkish-white, bell-shaped flowers. It usually grows in rocky recesses on coastal cliffs, though it can occur on tiled roofs; higher-altitude communities suggest its distribution may be broader than currently known.

A small annual daisy native to Mediterranean countries eastward to Iran. It is often slightly hairy, with a few small leaves that may be toothed or grow on the flower stem, and has finely short-haired seeds.
Evergreen herb or shrub native to Africa, widespread in forest regions from eastern Sudan to southern Angola. It is often sticky and has pale to dark purple or blue flowers with white throats.

A flowering shrub or small tree native to the Andes of Ecuador and Colombia, it is now extinct in the wild. It bears hanging, fragrant, yellow trumpet-shaped flowers and remains widely cultivated as an ornamental.
edibilityNote: All parts of the plant are poisonous.

summary: Bush or small tree endemic to Ecuador and listed as Extinct in the Wild since March 2014. Its exceptionally large, hanging trumpet-shaped flowers open white and may remain white or age to peach, pink or apricot.
edibilityNote: Flowers, leaves and seeds are exceptionally poisonous in large quantities; swallowing them is likely to cause severe neurological and physical symptoms.

summary: Flowering plant endemic to Madeira. It is protected under Portuguese or European legislation.
A flowering plant native from the Caucasus through Central Asia to the western Himalaya. It tolerates poor soil, drought and nearby paving, making it suitable as a street tree.
An evergreen, branched shrub endemic to Madeira. It has leathery, spoon-shaped to broad-tipped leaves and small white flowers spotted pink to red, blooming from October to June.
A flowering plant endemic to Portugal’s Madeira Archipelago. It is protected under Portuguese or European Community legislation, specifically Annexes II and IV of the Habitats Directive.

A tropical tree native to the Atlantic Forest from Rio de Janeiro to southeastern Minas Gerais, Chrysophyllum imperiale is endangered following habitat loss. It has large pale leaves and solid oval yellow fruits, which were much appreciated by Brazilian emperors Pedro I and Pedro II.
edibilityNote: The yellow fruits were historically much appreciated by Brazilian emperors Pedro I and Pedro II.

summary: Flowering plant endemic to Madeira. It is protected under Annexes II and IV of the Habitats Directive.

Plant endemic to mainland Portugal, restricted to south-facing limestone coastal cliffs between Sesimbra and Cape Espichel. In the 2020 mainland assessment, only about 500 mature plants and two locations were estimated, and it was assessed as Endangered following recent declines in habitat quality and plant numbers.

sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

summary: Flowering plant found in Portugal; the subspecies Crambe fruticosa subsp. fruticosa is endemic to Madeira.
A mustard-family plant endemic to the Canary Islands. It has rough, stalked leaves with blunt teeth, while its stems are more or less smooth.
A hawthorn native to the Mediterranean Basin. Wild plants produce plentiful, unusually plump haw fruits, while different varieties have orange, yellowish or red-tinged fruit.
Evergreen tree native to eastern and southern Asia. New leaves are deep purple-crimson before becoming glossy green above and blue-green below, while its acorn cups have distinctive concentric rings.
edibilityNote: Acorns are edible; dried, ground acorns can be mixed with cereals as flour, and roasted seeds can substitute for coffee.

summary: A slow-growing succulent shrub native to northwestern and north-central Namibia, it has a swollen base, large shiny leaves and grape-like fruits. It sheds its leaves during the drier winter, and its fruits are extremely poisonous.
edibilityNote: The grape-like fruits are extremely poisonous and should be avoided.

summary: A small or medium-sized deciduous tree endemic to China. It sheds its leaves around December in the Northern Hemisphere and remains dormant through winter. Its valuable rosewood was used in Chinese furniture, and heavy exploitation left most commercially sized trees cut down by the early twenty-first century.
A herbaceous plant native to Taiwan and the Chinese areas of Guangdong, Hong Kong and Hainan. Its fruits are berries.

A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It grows in Mediterranean temporary pools and other seasonally flooded places, especially on siliceous soils and occasionally on calcium-depleted limestone soils.

Flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula, Eryngium galioides is associated with temporary pools and other seasonally waterlogged wetlands. In mainland Portugal, assessments conducted from 2016 to 2019 classified it as Vulnerable amid continuing habitat decline and threats including agricultural expansion, drainage and prolonged droughts.
