summary: An aquatic plant native to Australia, it occurs most commonly in shallow, stagnant water. Its whorled leaves change from thread-like underwater forms to thicker intermediate leaves and smooth linear forms, and its female flowers lack petals.

An herbaceous biennial native to the western and central Mediterranean Basin, it occurs across southern Europe and North Africa. Its two accepted subspecies have partly separate ranges, one mainly European and the other spanning Spain and northwestern Africa.
Plant native to France, Spain and Portugal, naturalized in the United Kingdom and cultivated elsewhere. It is also sometimes treated as a subspecies of another daffodil.

An aquatic perennial found mainly in western Europe, with scattered populations elsewhere, including North Africa and Newfoundland. It grows from creeping underground stems in shallow, nutrient-poor water and produces delicate submerged leaves that usually decay after its floating leaves appear.

An orchid native to Asia Minor and parts of Europe and North Africa, the dense-flowered orchid forms a basal rosette of oblong leaves above round underground nodules. From April to June, upright stems bear clusters of small white to pink flowers.
An orchid native to the Mediterranean Basin and Europe’s Atlantic coast. Its flower spike carries greyish-pink flowers whose sepals and petals form a hood.
Highly variable orchid native to Europe and the Middle East. Its flowers resemble spiders, with yellow-green sepals and a velvety red-brown lip marked by a distinctive silvery-blue H.

A flowering plant with no explicitly stated native origin, it is found from Mexico and the West Indies to subtropical South America. It grows in habitats ranging from tropical savanna and forest to mountains, shrubland and grassland, and has not been documented north of Mexico.

Evergreen perennial native to Argentina and Chile, with clumps of grey-green, sword-shaped leaves. Its creamy white, cup-shaped flowers have golden centres and bloom from May to June in the Northern Hemisphere.

A hardy flowering bulb native to the Pyrenees of southwestern France and northwestern Spain, it bears deep purple early-summer flowers with yellow markings. Its stiff, sword-shaped dark green to teal leaves begin growing in early spring, before the snow has fully melted.

Bulbous flowering plant native to eastern South Africa, Lesotho and Eswatini, where it grows in wet areas near streams, marshes and drainages. It has lance-shaped leaves and deep orange to orange-brown flowers, and has escaped cultivation and become established in parts of the United Kingdom.

Creeping flowering herb native from western Asia through India to East and Southeast Asia. It resembles a true strawberry but has yellow flowers, while the common variety bears glossy red fruit. Its fresh berries are edible but less palatable than true strawberries.
edibilityNote: Fresh berries are edible but less palatable than true strawberries; Khasi people also chew the roots with betel nuts.

summary: A moss with a cosmopolitan distribution across climates ranging from the Arctic to deserts. When wet, it is bright green with loose leaves; when dry, the leaves wrap around its stems and turn reddish brown. It can remain dormant through years of drying and resume activity after rehydration.

A bulb-bearing herbaceous perennial native to the western Mediterranean region of Iberia, Italy and northwest Africa. It produces a dense, pyramid-shaped cluster of numerous blue flowers; its foliage dies back in summer and reappears in autumn.
A flowering bromeliad native to Chile. It can grow on other plants or in well-drained soil, and bears edible fruits resembling those of Greigia sphacelata but smaller, eaten in the same way.
edibilityNote: The smaller fruits resemble those of Greigia sphacelata and are eaten in the same way.

summary: A sedge with no stated native origin, it occurs from Western Asia through southern Europe to northwest Africa. It grows on rocky and grassy slopes.

A perennial shrub native to Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Venezuela. Its clustered tubular flowers gradually change from yellow to red, creating a marmalade-like display against dark green oval or elliptical leaves.
Fern native from the southern United States through Mexico, the Caribbean and Central America to western South America. It grows in rocky hammocks and moist forests.

Herbaceous perennial tuberous plant native to the Mediterranean region, the poppy anemone bears single, showy flowers with black centres. Wild flowers are usually red but may be white or blue, blooming from winter to early spring in their native range.

A highly variable tree occurring along Australia’s east coast, coastal banksia ranges from a small, gnarled shrub in exposed sites to a tall tree in shelter. Its leaves contrast dark green upper surfaces with white undersides, and its densely packed flower spikes are usually pale yellow to yellow.
edibilityNote: Historically, Indigenous Australians consumed its nectar by licking stroked hands or steeping flower spikes overnight; early settlers used the nectar as syrup.

summary: A semi-evergreen, clump-forming perennial native to western Europe, including Britain, France, Spain and Portugal. Its long, narrow leaves are usually spotted white or pale green, while its spring flowers change from pink to blue or violet.

A parasitic herb recorded in eastern and northern Xinjiang, Central Asia, southwestern Asia and Europe. It parasitizes bedstraw species and bears spikes of yellow, glandular-hairy flowers from May to July.

sources.title: Orobanche caryophyllacea in Flora of China @ efloras.org

summary: A flowering parasitic plant considered indigenous in Switzerland and distributed across southern Europe. It grows on Artemisia campestris and has yellow-to-violet stems with white-to-pale-yellow flowers marked by violet veins.

sources.title: Orobanche artemisiae-campestris Gaudin
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: Annual herb native to coastal western Europe, where it grows on sandy dunes and heaths. It forms low, greyish, hairy rosettes with pale, usually paired flowers; its fruits resemble tiny storks’ bills and open to reveal feathery seed appendages.
A short-lived flowering plant whose subspecies littorale is native to mainland Portugal. The species is terrestrial and associated with sunny European places, especially coastal ones.

sources.title: Centaurium littorale (Turner) Gilmour
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A perennial flowering herb native to Atlantic Europe, including England, western France and the northwestern Iberian Peninsula, it grows on coastal cliffs and dune grassland. It was assessed as Endangered in 2001.

A flowering plant found around the Mediterranean Basin and extending into northwestern Europe. Its upper leaves join around the stiff stems, and it bears bright yellow flowers. It grows in chalk or limestone grassland and on dunes.

A flowering plant found mainly in western and Mediterranean Europe and also in southern Australia. Its four-petalled yellow flowers, sometimes tinged pink, open only in sunlight, and it grows around seasonally flooded pools and on sandy or peaty acid grassland.

A flowering plant indigenous to Switzerland, with a wider Eurasian distribution. It has a garlic-like smell, hairy stems, toothed oval leaves and pink flowers, and grows in wet places such as fens, ditches and shores.

sources.title: Teucrium scordium L.
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A succulent perennial endemic to central Mexico’s Sierra Mixteca. Its branched stems may stand upright or spread along the ground, while its blue-grey, cylindrical leaves develop reddish tips in dry conditions.

A mat-forming perennial herb native to Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean. Its stems root at their joints, enabling it to spread vegetatively into dense ground cover that can prevent other plants from regenerating.
A perennial herb native to the Caribbean and South America. Its banana-like leaves accompany upright flower clusters with red bracts and pale-yellow tubular flowers.

A small evergreen perennial native to Japan, where it grows on open and forested slopes. It forms grasslike leaf tufts above short rhizomes and bears purple or white flowers; the ‘Kokuryu’ cultivar develops nearly black leaves and black berries.
A large, tree-like yucca of the far southeastern Chihuahuan Desert, occurring in northeastern Mexico. It may branch and bears snowy white flowers.
A cactus native to central Mexico, it forms dense clusters of elongated stems covered in very sharp yellow or brown spines. White or yellow flowers appear from late winter to early summer.

A cactus from the Mexican states of San Luis Potosí, Querétaro, Guanajuato, Puebla and Oaxaca, it grows in oak forests and grasslands. Its rounded body bears curved yellow-to-red spines, and striking pink flowers appear from early spring to summer.
Cactus native to northern and southern Mexico. It bears bell-shaped purplish-pink to red flowers in winter and early spring, and its curved spines were traditionally used as fishing hooks.

A flowering cactus native to central Mexico, usually forming clumps but sometimes growing alone. It has long white spines, white wool and blue-green tissue, with crowns of carmine-pink flowers followed by small, tart, technically edible fruits.
edibilityNote: The small fruits are described as technically edible, with a tart, fruity flavour; only animal consumption is specifically reported.

summary: A cactus occurring in the Mexican states of Nuevo León, Coahuila and Tamaulipas. It usually grows alone, with flattened spherical blue-green or pale-green stems, strong central spines but no outer spines, and yellowish-white flowers followed by red fruits.

A cactus found in the southwestern United States and northern Mexico, it has a conspicuous shrub-like or tree-like form with sharply barbed spines. Its yellowish, lumpy fruits are retained throughout winter and are often mistaken for flowers.
edibilityNote: The dry, bland fruits are said to have been eaten by Indigenous people in Arizona and New Mexico.

summary: An epiphytic cactus native to southern Mexico, where it inhabits cloud forests in the Sierra Madre de Oaxaca and Chiapas Highlands. Its flattened, leaf-like stems arch downward, and it bears large scarlet, funnel-shaped flowers with greenish throats.

A succulent cactus native to the Mexican states of Hidalgo, Guanajuato and Querétaro, it forms clusters of bluish-green stems with white spines and yellow flowers. Its gracilis subspecies produces abundant offsets that detach easily, while the two recognized subspecies differ noticeably in their spines and flowers.
A flowering agave native to central, northeastern and southwestern Mexico.

A giant succulent native to the Mexican states of Oaxaca, Puebla and Veracruz, it forms a massive rosette of exceptionally large leaves. After many years, each rosette produces one towering branched flower stalk whose flowers open red and turn yellow, then fruits and dies.
edibilityNote: It is used for pulque and is also collected from the wild to make mezcal.

summary: A perennial succulent shrub native to tropical and subtropical North and Central America, Devil’s Backbone has smooth leaves and bright red, slipper-shaped bracts. It generally flowers in mid-spring, and its flowers have no scent.
edibilityNote: Roots, stems and leaves are toxic; swallowing root juice or even a few seeds can cause severe vomiting and diarrhea.

summary: Fast-growing leafy perennial shrub native to Mexico and believed to have originated from the Yucatán Peninsula through Central America to Panama. Damaged plants release irritating, often toxic latex, and some varieties have stinging hairs. Young leaves and tender stem tips are eaten cooked, but raw leaves contain toxic cyanogenic compounds, so thorough cooking is essential.
edibilityNote: Young leaves and tender stem tips are eaten boiled, steamed or stir-fried; raw leaves are toxic, and thorough cooking is essential.

summary: A perennial stonecrop from northeastern Mexico, it has many branching stems and rosettes of thick, grey-green, spoon-shaped leaves. This highly variable plant bears upright, loosely clustered orange-yellow flowers and is widely grown ornamentally.

A succulent native to Tamaulipas, Mexico. Its powdery leaf coating gives it a ghostlike appearance, while its thick leaves detach easily from the rosette and its spring flowers are white with red spots. It is used as an edible vegetable.
edibilityNote: Plants of this species are used as edible vegetables.

summary: A flowering succulent native to Tamaulipas, Mexico, it forms a rosette of pinkish-white leaves and bears red flowers. The ‘Topsy Turvy’ cultivar originated in California and has leaves positioned upside-down.

A pine tree native to the highlands of Mexico, it has long grass-green needles that droop with a weeping effect. Its pale pink to salmon timber is moderately soft and brittle, with a strong aniseed smell when freshly cut.

A rainforest vine found from southern Mexico south to Panama, though the supplied information does not explicitly identify its native range. It climbs by roots and bears very large, triangular leaves that are often cut almost to the central rib.

A plant native from southern Mexico to Ecuador. It is cold-hardy in cultivation, but is unlikely to flower after freezing back to the ground. Traditional uses include treating asthma, diabetes, fever, headaches and several other ailments.

A perennial insect-eating herb native to El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras and Mexico, it changes from sticky, prey-catching summer leaves to small non-carnivorous winter leaves. Pink, purple or violet flowers appear twice a year.
Tree native to Central America, commonly known as the tree fuchsia.
Small shrub of unknown origin, distributed in Asia and Mexico. Its terminal flower clusters are yellow with red at the base, and it grows beside streams in mountain, oak and pine forests.

A submerged, free-floating aquatic plant of unspecified native origin, it has been reported across parts of Europe, Asia, Africa, the Middle East, Florida and the Dominican Republic. Its leaves divide three or four times into threadlike tips, distinguishing it from rigid hornwort.

An agave found in central Mexico, forming a single open rosette of thick, light-green to yellow-green leaves with strong dark-brown tip spines. Its tall, narrow flower cluster bears blossoms that are reddish-purple at first and yellow when open.

A succulent of unstated native origin, it is recorded in the Mexican states of Hidalgo, Puebla and Veracruz. This stemless plant forms a cluster of leathery grey-green to green leaves, with a tall flower stalk bearing a red stem and red bracts.

A cactus native to the Baja California peninsula, it forms a richly branched shrub or small tree with blue-green branches. Its pale greenish-white flowers open by day and night, and its spherical red fruits are edible.
edibilityNote: The spherical red fruits are edible.

summary: A large shrubby cactus native to central and northern Mexico, developing candelabra-like branches when mature. Its creamy-white flowers last less than a day. Its dark-purple berries are edible and sold for consumption in Mexico.
edibilityNote: The dark-purple berries are edible and sold for consumption in Mexico.

summary: Solitary or branching cactus native only to Mexico, specifically limestone hills and dry forest in Hidalgo, Guanajuato, Querétaro and San Luis Potosí. It has blue-green, frosted, ribbed stems with yellow spines. Its bell-shaped yellow flowers are followed by pale, fleshy fruits tinged red.
A fern indigenous to the Neotropical Caribbean and Amazon rainforest, and to the Azores. It is known as the mossy finger fern.
A cactus native to Oaxaca, Mexico, it has slender stems with about seven ribs and numerous needle-like spines. Flowers grow at the stem tips, followed by round, somewhat flattened fruits.
A cactus of unstated native origin, listed in CITES Appendix II. Its flowers are visited by broad-billed hummingbirds.
A prickly pear native to the tropical and subtropical Americas. It usually has more than three spines at each spine-bearing spot, distinguishing it from Opuntia stricta.

A shrubby cactus native to Coahuila, Mexico, it forms broad clumps of round to wedge-shaped green or blue-green stem segments. It bears up to six yellow or reddish needle-like spines and large yellow flowers flushed with red.

A low, mat-forming shrub cactus found in Baja California Sur, Mexico, at elevations up to 50 metres, Opuntia pycnantha has densely spined, round to short-oblong stem sections. Its yellow flowers are flushed red, and its fruits are heavily spined.

A flowering cactus native to the Chihuahuan Desert of North America and parts of South America. In Queensland, Australia, it is an invasive agricultural weed whose long spines can painfully injure people and animals and damage vehicle tyres.

A prickly pear cactus occurring in Guatemala and southern Mexico, including the Yucatán dry forest. Its widely spreading branches bear slender flattened pads with several spines at each spine-bearing point, followed by yellow-to-rose flowers and red mature fruits.

A broadleaf red shrub native to Mexico and South America. It has purplish stems, small white flowers with creamy bracts and colourful foliage; broken stems release irritating, poisonous sap that can severely damage internal organs if swallowed.
edibilityNote: The sap is poisonous and can severely damage internal organs if ingested.

summary: Perennial herb native to the tropical Americas. Its arching stems hold conspicuous dense balls of flowers and fruit capsules away from the stem. Its milky sap can irritate skin and eyes.
A lycophyte native to Mexico and Central America, Selaginella martensii is commonly known as variegated spikemoss or Martens's spike moss.

A rhizomatous fern native to a broad area from northern Mexico to eastern Brazil, it has fan-shaped pale- or dark-green fronds with spore structures along their divisions. It favours humid tropical settings and low light in cultivation but does not tolerate cool temperatures.
A flowering succulent native to central Mexico, specifically Puebla and Veracruz. It forms clustered rosettes of pointed green leaves with red margins and bears yellow flowers.

A succulent native to Mexico, it grows naturally on rocky ground and cliff faces. Its evergreen leaves are bright orange-copper and may develop red or orange edges in strong sun, while white star-shaped flowers bloom in spring.
edibilityNote: It is not listed as toxic by the ASPCA, but no human food use is documented.

summary: A flowering plant endemic to Portugal’s Madeira Archipelago.

A trailing succulent perennial native to southern Mexico, burro’s-tail is known in the wild from two ravines in central Veracruz and nearby vertical volcanic cliffs. It has fleshy blue-green leaves and summer flowers ranging from pink to red; its fragile leaves detach easily but can readily form roots and new plants.
A perennial succulent native to Mexico, it grows on rocks at higher elevations. It has thick, flattened purplish or bluish-green leaves and dark red flowers in summer.

Succulent species reported as native to Nuevo León in northern Mexico. It forms symmetrical rosettes of fleshy, silvery-grey leaves and produces pale pink or coral flowers from late winter to early spring.

A flowering perennial native to Chiapas, Mexico, it naturally grows on other plants in wet forests and cloudy highland settings. Its deep forest-green, velvety, heart-shaped leaves have striking ivory to light-green veins, and it produces orange berries.
edibilityNote: Poisonous to humans when ingested; calcium oxalate crystals in the leaves can cause mouth and throat pain, nausea, swallowing difficulty and other symptoms.

summary: A tropical palm native to Madagascar, it forms multiple cane-like stems and upward-curving leaves that create a butterfly-like outline. Its fruit ripens from yellow or gold to dark purple or black, and it is widely grown as an ornamental or houseplant.

A desert plant native to the Chihuahuan Desert and other dry habitats of northern and central Mexico, it forms a symmetrical rosette of firm, narrow leaves. In midsummer it produces a towering spike of small white flowers.

A trunk-forming plant found in Mexico's Zacatecas and Coahuila, growing on open ground, gypsum dunes and rocky slopes. Its dense, waxy blue leaves have upward-pointing marginal spines, while tall, narrow flower stalks carry green to cream flowers.

An evergreen epiphytic perennial native to rainforest habitats from southern Mexico and Central America into northern and central South America. Its foliage forms a star-shaped rosette topped by orange and red bracts; cultivated varieties may flower in maroon, red, orange, yellow or pink.

Perennial herb originally native only to South America. Its creeping rhizome produces dense rows of stems and turf-like growth; unusually for a rush, it often occupies very dry Andean roadsides and abandoned fields.

A bulbous perennial endemic to South Africa’s Cape Province, it bears long-lasting white or cream flowers whose brown or green centres fade with age. The flowers turn toward the sun, while the fleshy leaves die after flowering.

An evergreen tropical shrub or small tree native throughout Mexico and Central America. It has glossy, willow-like leaves, funnel-shaped yellow flowers and deep red-black fruit; all parts are toxic to most vertebrates, and many human poisonings are known.
edibilityNote: All parts are toxic, and human poisonings include intentional swallowing of the seeds.

summary: A slow-growing flowering epiphyte native to southern Mexico, El Salvador, Guatemala and Honduras. Its broad greenish-silver leaves form a sculptural rosette, and its red-purple tubular flowers have petals that last for months.

An evergreen perennial herb endemic to dry areas of Nuevo León in northeastern Mexico, woolly spiderwort has fleshy leaves arranged in a precise geometric pattern. Greyish-white hairs cover almost the entire plant, contrasting with its bright purplish-pink or purple three-petalled flowers.

An evergreen perennial subshrub native to the tropical Americas, from Mexico through Central America and the Caribbean to Bolivia and southern Brazil. Its fruit capsule is enclosed by a fleshy purple-black covering, giving it a berry-like appearance; a variegated form called ‘Mexican Flag’ is grown ornamentally.
A herb native to tropical America. Its arrow-shaped leaves have a bluish tone; both the leaves and rhizome can be eaten after cooking.
edibilityNote: The leaves and rhizome are eaten cooked.

summary: A herbaceous ornamental plant whose native origin is not stated in the supplied information. Its summer display has a mauve to rose-purple sheath with pale margins around a yellow spike. The green, unmarked leaves are semi-erect and not arrow-shaped like those of other species.

A perennial flowering plant native to Mexico, Colombia and Central America. It has large, bright pink, funnel-shaped flowers and green strap-like leaves, and commonly blooms soon after heavy rain. It contains toxic alkaloids; ingestion can cause vomiting, convulsions and death.
edibilityNote: The plant contains toxic alkaloids; ingestion can cause vomiting, convulsions and death.

summary: A terrestrial bromeliad occurring from Mexico to Brazil, with no native origin specified. Its serrated leaves form a rosette, while its many-flowered cluster has a very short stalk, red bracts and pink petals.

summary: A bushy shrub native from New Guinea to Queensland, Australia. It has alternate, long-stalked leaves and white flowers with five petals, and is often grown as an ornamental.
A flowering plant native to Oaxaca and Chiapas in Mexico, eyelash begonia is a popular houseplant available in several cultivars.
Flowering begonia native to Mexico and Central America. Its rhizome grows upward rather than along the ground, and pink or white flowers appear in winter.
Flowering plant native to southeastern Mexico, where it grows in extremely dense shade in tropical forests.
A perennial flowering plant native from Mexico to Colombia, growing mainly in wet tropical habitats.
edibilityNote: Documented as used for food; no edible part, preparation or historical context is supplied.

summary: An evergreen shrub or small tree native to mainland China. Its spiny compound leaves are joined by fragrant yellow flowers in late winter and early spring, followed by grape-like clusters of blue-black, wax-coated berries.
edibilityNote: Berries are used in preserves, drinks and sweets, usually cooked or sweetened; flowers and simmered young leaves are also eaten.

summary: A flowering plant native to southern Mexico and Central America, Centradenia inaequilateralis has pink-purple flowers. Its cultivar ‘Cascade’ has received the Royal Horticultural Society’s Award of Garden Merit.

A small tree native to Brazil, strawberry guava has oval leaves and thin-skinned fruit ranging from yellow to dark red or purple. Its juicy fruit and skin are edible, fresh or made into jam and juice, although removing the skin gives a sweeter flavour. It is highly invasive in many tropical regions.
edibilityNote: The fruit's skin and juicy interior are edible; it is eaten fresh or made into jam and juice, sometimes after removing the skin.

summary: A shrub or woody-based plant native to tropical America, it grows wild beside roads and in disturbed vegetation across several forest types. It is heavily branched, with broad leaves and upright pale-green or yellowish flower spikes; its fruits turn black when dry.
An evergreen shrub from New Guinea and the Solomon Islands. It has flattened, jointed green stems and arrow-shaped leaves, with both spreading and climbing growth.

A shrub or small tree from much of Central and South America, especially Mexico and Guatemala; its natural habitat includes seasonally dry tropical forest slopes in the Sierra Madre Occidental. It has fragrant white, funnel-shaped flowers and ribbed capsules containing winged seeds. Its dried bark is traditionally brewed as tea and consumed as both a food beverage and household remedy.
edibilityNote: Dried bark is brewed as tea, traditionally consumed in Central and South America as both a food beverage and household remedy.

sources.title: Hintonia latiflora (Sessé & Moc. ex DC.) Bullock

summary: A shrub or tree native from Mexico to northwestern Colombia. It grows mainly in wet tropical regions and is used medicinally.

summary: Evergreen perennial endemic to Guizhou and Yunnan in southern China and to Vietnam. Its dark-green oval leaves have slightly textured or serrated edges and four raised silvery patches, while underground rhizomes help it spread.

An evergreen climber native to tropical West Africa, with opposite pairs of oval to oblong leaves. Its striking flower clusters combine red petals with white to pale-purple outer cups, making it a popular ornamental in frost-free conditions.

Tree native to the Magellanic and Valdivian temperate forests of Chile and Argentina. It has glossy green leaves with whitish undersides, creamy white fragrant flowers and bluish berries. Indigenous people historically ate its astringent bark, which is also used as a pepper substitute in Argentina and Chile.
edibilityNote: Indigenous people historically ate the astringent bark; it is also used as a pepper substitute in Argentina and Chile.

summary: Perennial herb native to South America. Its slightly wavy, variegated leaves may be green, red, yellow or mixtures of these colours, making it popular as an ornamental edging plant. Its edible leaves are also harvested from the wild.
edibilityNote: The edible leaves are harvested from the wild.

summary: Neotropical mistletoe native to Colombia, Mexico, the Mexican Gulf and Venezuela. It has hairless branches, opposite leaves and terminal groups of three yellow-to-scarlet flowers, each above a cup-shaped bract.

A deciduous tree native to tropical and subtropical South America, it may grow as a tree or shrub depending on water availability. It has dense, zigzagging branches with strong spines. Its sweet but scarcely fleshy fruits are edible, although there is no market or habit of human consumption.
edibilityNote: The sweet, scarcely fleshy fruits are edible, but there is no market or habit of human consumption.

summary: A highly branched shrub or subshrub native and endemic to Mexico, it grows mainly in high-mountain grasslands and open pine forest. Its densely woolly foliage is aromatic when crushed, and it bears bright yellow flower heads.
Aromatic shrub endemic to Mexico. It bears rounded, lobed leaves and yellow flower clusters, blooming in the dry season, roughly November to March.

A tufted perennial sedge with underground stems, native to parts of southern North America, most of Central America and northern South America. Its flowering heads have pale or whitish, egg-shaped spikelets packed into clusters.

sources.title: Cyperus luzulae Rottler
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A perennial chilli shrub originating in ancient Peru and across the Andean region of South America, it has white or cream flowers and usually downward-hanging pods with citrus or fruity flavours. Heat varies widely among cultivars. Ají amarillo is used fresh in Peru and dried and ground in Bolivia.
edibilityNote: Ají amarillo is used as a condiment, mostly fresh in Peru and dried and ground in Bolivia.

summary: An evergreen shrub or small tree native to the South American Andes of Argentina, Bolivia and Peru, tamarillo grows quickly but is relatively short-lived. Its edible fruit is eaten fresh or made into juice, preserves, fruit salad and sauces, although unripe fruit is slightly toxic.
edibilityNote: The fruit is eaten fresh or prepared as juice, preserves, fruit salad and sauces; unripe fruit is slightly toxic.

summary: A shrub whose native origin is not stated, giant devil's-fig is found from Mexico to South America, including disturbed sites. It is recognized by its woolly, often rust-coloured covering and bears large velvety leaves, white flowers and green berries.

A flowering agave native to southern Mexico and Guatemala. This sterile hybrid is propagated vegetatively, usually from suckers, and bears narrow, toothed leaves ending in a strong spine. Its leaf fibre is used for rope, twine and other products.
edibilityNote: It is reported as an ingredient in traditional Mexican henequen liquor and mezcal.

summary: Succulent flowering plant native to Oaxaca and the area near Tehuacán in Puebla, Mexico. It forms a grey-green leaf rosette tipped with sharp black spines and bears small grey-and-red flowers on tall, sturdy stems.

Succulent plant native to Hidalgo, Tamaulipas, Guanajuato and Queretaro in Mexico. It forms a basal rosette of sword-shaped leaves with spiny, undulating margins, and produces tall stalks bearing greenish flowers.
An upright shrub native to Central America, firespike has glossy opposite leaves and terminal spikes of waxy red to burgundy flowers. It blooms in summer and autumn and is sensitive to frost.

A perennial herb or undershrub native to southeastern Africa, with narrow, lance-shaped leaves. Widely grown as an ornamental, it also feeds monarch butterfly caterpillars, which retain the plant's toxic compounds as a defence against predators.
edibilityNote: All parts can be toxic if swallowed, affecting the heart, breathing, nervous system and stomach; sap can also injure the eyes.

summary: A semi-deciduous flowering tree native to Central and South America, it forms a broad, symmetrical umbrella-shaped crown. Its leaves fold in rainy weather and at night, while its pods contain sticky edible pulp that can be made into a lemon-flavoured drink.
edibilityNote: The pod pulp is edible and made into a lemon-flavoured beverage; in Cambodia, fruit and, during famines, young leaves are eaten.

summary: An evergreen shrub growing naturally in Vanuatu and occurring across the Pacific Islands. Its broad, sometimes crinkled leaves are coppery green with red splashes, and fine hairs cover both leaves and branches. Male flowers hang in long spikes, while the shorter female spikes are often hidden among the foliage.

A tuberous flowering plant native to Brazil, Sinningia speciosa produces large, velvety, brightly coloured flowers and is a popular houseplant. It often becomes dormant, when its tuber is kept cool and dry until growth resumes.

A scrambling perennial plant native from Mexico and the Caribbean through Central and South America to Argentina and Bolivia. It may creep over the ground or climb trees as a woody vine, bearing yellow flower heads and narrow fruits tipped with two backward-barbed points.

Perennial deciduous legume shrub or small tree native to southern North America, the Caribbean and most of South America. It has dense foliage, clusters of small white flowers and seed pods that turn from green to brown. Unlike most plants formerly placed in Acacia, it is thornless.
edibilityNote: The bark is used to produce alcoholic beverages, and the root is used in Mexican pulque.

summary: A tree-shaped cactus of unstated native origin, found in parts of Mexico, coastal Venezuela, Colombia and the Dutch Caribbean. Its white flowers open at night and last until midday; its variably coloured, thorn-covered fruits shed their thorns when ripe and contain red flesh.
edibilityNote: The fruit is eaten by humans and described as good tasting.

summary: A tree-like cactus found in the Mexican states of Puebla, Tlaxcala and Oaxaca. Its pads bear silky white-to-yellow hairs, while its flowers are pink to reddish purple. The round red fruits are edible but covered with spines, hairs and tiny barbed bristles.
edibilityNote: The round red fruits are edible but bear spines, hairs and tiny barbed bristles.

sources.title: Opuntia pilifera F.A.C.Weber
sources.attribution: Döring M (2022). German Wikipedia - Species Pages. Wikimedia Foundation. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/4wn9dt accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A herb native to mainland Portugal. It grows in damp, nutrient-enriched vegetation beside streams, lagoons and reservoirs.
A fern native to South America.

A Mexican succulent native to the Durango–Sinaloa border and Chihuahua in the Sierra Madre Occidental, Echeveria affinis also occasionally occurs in San Luis Potosí. It grows at high elevations in rocky, very dry places and is adapted to poor, mineral-rich soils.

A succulent flowering plant native to the rocky canyons and arid hillsides of central Mexico. It forms a small, usually solitary rosette of thick, pointed green leaves; some varieties develop red or bronze tips, while summer flowers may be pink, orange or red.

A succulent native to Mexico and endemic to its Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt. It is fleshy and hairy throughout, with rosettes of green or brown leaves and intense red tubular flowers in autumn and winter.

Flowering plant found in the Mexican states of Puebla and Oaxaca. It forms large rosettes of broad green leaves edged in purple-red, followed by a tall branching display of pink flowers from September to October.

A succulent flowering plant native to Mexico, where it is widespread and fairly common in northern Oaxaca and southern Puebla. Its purplish striped leaves, knobby stems and seasonal flowers make it distinctive.
A flowering succulent native to southwestern and central Mexico.
A succulent flowering plant native to Mexico, it has also been introduced to the Dominican Republic, New Zealand and Vietnam.
An ornamental terrestrial herb occurring from Mexico to Venezuela and Bolivia and capable of growing in wet places. Its dried fruit is used as a rattle.
edibilityNote: The sap is drunk as a beverage; no preparation details are supplied.

sources.title: Alonsoa meridionalis (L.fil.) Kuntze
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A large, thorny climber native to South Africa and Mozambique. Its downward-pointing thorns help anchor climbing shoots, while fragrant white flowers are followed by bright red berries that attract birds.
A flowering bromeliad native to Central America and western Mexico, reaching as far north as Sinaloa.

sources.title: Billbergia pallidiflora Liebmann
sources.attribution: Döring M (2022). English Wikipedia - Species Pages. Wikimedia Foundation. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/c3kkgh accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: An ornamental plant from Latin America. Its large heart- or lance-shaped leaves have striking green, white, pink and red blotches. All parts are poisonous if eaten, causing mouth burning and swelling, nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea.
edibilityNote: All parts are poisonous; ingestion can cause mouth burning and swelling, nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea.

summary: A small palm native to rainforests in southern Mexico and Guatemala, the parlour palm has a slender green trunk and flexible, spineless stems. It can begin flowering while still unusually small, producing clusters of tiny yellow to orange-red scented flowers.

A climbing plant found from Mexico to Central America. Its young, waxy leaves overlap like shingles as it grows along the ground; on reaching a tree trunk, it climbs using anchoring roots and develops larger adult leaves.

A palm-like, rhizomatous plant endemic to Mexico, it forms tree-like rosettes whose numerous mature leaves remain attached to the stem. Its upright flower clusters appear whitish-yellow from a distance and bear small, separate male or female flowers.

An aquatic perennial reported as native from Mexico through Central America and separately in eastern and southern Brazil. It grows along rivers, lagoons, ponds and swamps, bearing dense groups of lilac or rarely white flowers.

An aquatic perennial native to Eurasia and North Africa, growing in relatively deep, still or slow-flowing calcareous fresh water. Its large, translucent, shiny leaves have distinctive net-like veins, and it has no floating leaves.

sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

summary: A fan palm native to southern China and northern Vietnam. It grows in multi-stemmed clumps with glossy, deeply divided evergreen leaves and bamboo-like trunks exposed as old fibrous sheaths fall away.

A large palm native to the Lesser Antilles, Colombia, Venezuela, and Trinidad and Tobago, it has a pale trunk topped by a green crownshaft. Its angled leaflets give the fronds a bottlebrush appearance, and its ripe fruit is purplish-black. The terminal bud is edible, while immature flower clusters have historically been pickled as a vegetable and young-flower sap fermented into alcohol.
edibilityNote: The terminal bud is edible; immature flower clusters were historically pickled, and sap from young flower clusters can be fermented into alcohol.

summary: A tree native from Mexico to Nicaragua, and perhaps Costa Rica, Bocconia arborea grows in temperate areas associated with seasonal and irrigated crops. It has deeply cut leaves with brownish or grey felted undersides and small, dark, glossy seeds.

A grass-like iris-family wildflower native to Mexico, Central America and South America. Its flowers are often white with blue or purple centres but may also be yellow, pink or violet, followed by rounded brown seed capsules.
An orchid whose native status is not stated, found from north-central and southern Mexico through Central America.

A herbaceous perennial native to parts of Mexico, the Caribbean and northern South America. Its glossy, deeply veined leaves arch from the base, while its cream flower spike and white surrounding bract turn green with age.

A flowering plant that grows on other plants, native to Central America and Mexico. Thick, twisting leaves covered with fine gray hairs rise from a swollen base, and the plant bears red flower clusters with bright violet flowers.
A flowering plant endemic to Mexico.
A flowering plant native to southern Mexico, Central America, Colombia and Venezuela. It has long, lance-shaped leaves and yellow flowers marked with brown spots.

Robust herbaceous plant native to central Mexico and Central America. It can reach four metres, with huge waxy green leaves and flower structures combining a white to yellowish-green sheath with a pale yellow to ochre central spike.
edibilityNote: The plant is described generally as a food source; no part or preparation is specified.

summary: An orchid of unstated native origin, widespread across much of Mexico south to Costa Rica.

sources.title: Guarianthe aurantiaca (Bateman ex Lindl.) Dressler & W.E.Higgins
sources.attribution: Döring M (2022). English Wikipedia - Species Pages. Wikimedia Foundation. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/c3kkgh accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A tree of unspecified native origin, this species is reported from Mexico through Central America to Colombia, Venezuela, the Guianas, the Amazon, Peru and Brazil.

A begonia native to southeastern Brazil, where it grows beneath the Atlantic rainforest canopy. Its olive-green oblong leaves have silver spots and red-purple undersides, while its clustered flowers are white or pink with yellow centers.

An annual plant native to the Mediterranean and Asia, rocket has deeply lobed leaves and creamy-white flowers marked with purple veins. Its sharp-tasting leaves are widely eaten in salads, while its flowers, young seed pods and mature seeds are also edible.
edibilityNote: Leaves, flowers, young pods and mature seeds are edible; leaves are eaten raw or cooked, and aged seed oil is used for salads and cooking.

summary: A vigorously climbing woody vine native to tropical Asia. Its fragrant tubular flowers open white at dusk, turn pink on the second day and red on the third, while changing from horizontal to drooping.

A climbing herb native to Mexico, El Salvador, Guatemala and Honduras. It often grows beside streams or in gallery forest in drier areas, and bears broad funnel-shaped flowers ranging from red to pale pink.

sources.title: Ipomoea pedicellaris Benth.
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A perennial herb or shrub native to Nicaragua, Costa Rica, Guatemala, El Salvador and Chiapas in Mexico. It has yellow-green leaves, sometimes with purple veins, and showy flowers ranging from bright red to pinkish cream, surrounded by contrasting colourful bracts and calyces.
Evergreen shrub native to Mexico, with cup-shaped scarlet flowers produced mainly in summer. It is cultivated as an ornamental plant and needs a warm, sheltered position in temperate areas.

A trailing plant native to South American tropical rainforest, it has hanging shoots and tiny, thick, fleshy, button-like leaves that may weave around one another. It can grow on trees, rocks, rotten logs or the forest floor, favouring moist, shaded conditions.

Plane tree endemic to northeastern Mexico, mainly parts of Nuevo León, San Luis Potosí and Tamaulipas. Its olive-green leaves turn yellow-green in winter, while white flowers bloom from December through February.

Perennial flowering climber native to Mexico, with isolated sightings elsewhere in tropical Central and South America. Its hooked tendrils cling to supports, while its large, scented, bell-shaped flowers open white and turn violet as they mature.

A flowering shrub or small tree native to the Americas from Mexico through Central America into South America, as well as the Caribbean. It is covered in spines and stinging hairs, with pink or purple flower clusters and spongy green or pinkish fruit.

A perennial herb native to southern Mexico, parts of the Caribbean, Central America, Colombia and Venezuela. It was historically used as a natural sweetener in Mexico and parts of Central America, although bitter compounds, especially camphor, have limited wider use.
edibilityNote: Historically used as a natural sweetener in Mexico and parts of Central America.

summary: A scrambling shrub native to southern and central Africa, Cape honeysuckle is normally evergreen but may lose its leaves in colder climates. Its narrow tubular flowers range from orange and orange-red to apricot, appearing at varying times but usually from autumn to spring.

A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. There it grows in rock crevices, scree and rocky or coarse sandy slopes, strictly on silica-rich ground. Its nonflowering branches may have opposite leaves arranged in four rows, but this feature requires confirmation.

An epiphyte or tree found from Mexico to Costa Rica and in the Antilles. It has cream-coloured latex and petals, while its rounded fruit remains green when mature. It grows in evergreen or secondary forests and along roadsides in the Atlantic zone.
Erect perennial shrub native to the Canary Islands. Its pale green leaves and stems have long white hairs, while its flowers range from pale purple to deep magenta.

A herbaceous perennial native to Puebla, Tamaulipas and Veracruz in Mexico, roseleaf sage grows in shady places such as forest edges. Its beetroot-red flowers are enclosed by large, colourful paired bracts, which fall away as the flowers expand.

A small to medium-sized tree native to rainforests of southeast Queensland and the extreme north of adjacent New South Wales, Australia. It has glossy leaves with wavy edges, white or pink flowers and rounded woody fruits that are edible.
edibilityNote: Its rounded woody fruits are edible.

summary: Evergreen shrub from Mexico, Mexican orange has three-part aromatic leaves that smell like basil when crushed, and scented white flowers in spring, sometimes followed by limited autumn flowering.
Shrub or small tree native to South and Southeast Asia, China and Australasia. It has fragrant white or cream flowers and orange-red berries containing hairy seeds.
Tree native to Bolivia, Peru, Mexico and the United States (Florida).

A shrub native to Central America, it occurs from Mexico to Costa Rica and sometimes grows on other plants. Its hanging flowers have pink-to-red tubes and green petals, while the elongated green berries develop purple speckles when ripe.

A bunchgrass widely distributed across Eurasia, Africa and the Americas, though its native geographic origin is not specified. It forms tight tufts of wiry leaves and delicate silvery or purplish flower heads on wavy, hair-like stalks.

An annual grass distributed around the Mediterranean and Middle East, with no native range explicitly stated. It has been widely introduced to drier regions worldwide. Compared with sea fern-grass, it has a more open flower cluster and a ridged flowering stalk.

A small tree or shrub native to Mexico, Montanoa bipinnatifida often grows in groups and sometimes flowers so young that it does not yet look woody. It has very large, opposite leaves deeply divided into toothed lobes, and broad, branching clusters of flower heads with white outer flowers and yellow centres.
A Mexican subshrub found in Jalisco, Zacatecas, Aguascalientes, Hidalgo, Guanajuato and San Luis Potosí. Its flower heads contain only disc flowers, with no ray flowers.

A herbaceous perennial native from Mexico through Central America to Colombia and Ecuador, tree dahlia has hollow, cane-like, four-sided stems and large leaves. Its nodding flowerheads are typically lavender or mauvish-pink.
edibilityNote: Petals can be eaten in salads or soups; Q'eqchi' people in San Pedro Carchá, Guatemala, use the leaves as a dietary supplement.

summary: Evergreen flowering shrub native to Mesoamerica and widespread from Tamaulipas in Mexico to Costa Rica. In autumn it bears fragrant, flat clusters of white-to-pink, daisy-like flowers that attract butterflies, above light-green toothed leaves.

An evergreen upright shrub endemic to Mexico's cloud forests. Its reddish-purple branches carry large, slightly rough dark-green leaves, while scented mauve, lilac or magenta-blue flower clusters appear in spring with a bursting-fireworks appearance.

An annual herb described as a North American species and widespread from Mexico through parts of Central and South America. Its finely divided leaves accompany many small, bright yellow flower heads. Its lemon-flavoured flowers are reported as edible garnishes, although the source flags this claim as needing a citation.
edibilityNote: The lemon-flavoured flowers are reported edible and used as garnish, but the source marks the claim as needing a citation.

summary: A semi-epiphytic shrub or vine of unspecified native origin, occurring from southern Mexico to Colombia and Ecuador. It has leathery leaves, striking orange tubular flowers and soft orange-yellow berries enclosed by the persistent flower cup.

An evergreen shrub presumed native to temperate Andean regions of Colombia, Peru and Chile, pepino is not known in the wild. It bears sweet edible fruit with melon-like colour and a flavour resembling honeydew and cucumber, often eaten fresh as a snack.
edibilityNote: The sweet, mild-flavoured fruit is often eaten fresh as a snack.

summary: Domesticated shrubby pepper native to Bolivia, Peru and Ecuador and known only in cultivation. Its hairy leaves and black seeds distinguish it from other peppers, while its variously coloured fruits range from mild to extremely hot.
edibilityNote: Fruits are eaten fresh, dried, ground or as paste; seeds and white membranes are often removed, and boiling can reduce their heat.

summary: Shrub native to Mexico, rosy cestrum has pink flowers.
A robust flowering vine native to Mexico, Central America and northwestern South America. Its long-lasting dark purple flowers eventually fade to white.
A tall, heavily branched yucca native to central Mexico, it bears straight leaves in rosette-shaped bunches at the end of each stem. Its hanging flower clusters contain many white flowers.

A succulent flowering plant native to central Mexico from Querétaro to Mexico State, thread agave forms a stemless rosette of dark to bronze-green leaves marked with ornamental white bud imprints. Its tall flower stalk bears densely packed yellowish-green to dark purple flowers in autumn and winter.

Small agave native to the Guadalajara region of Jalisco and the Ceboruco volcano area of Nayarit, Mexico. Its grey-green leaves bear distinctive overlap marks, large edge spines and a thick brown tip spine.

A trunk-forming agave of arid Puebla, Oaxaca and Veracruz in Mexico. It produces offshoots and has stiff green leaves with toothed edges and a dark-brown tip. Its tall, open flower cluster bears green to yellow flowers, typically from July to August.

A tree-like plant native to Texas and Mexico’s Chihuahua and Coahuila regions, it grows in desert, steppe and semiarid areas. Its trunk supports a crown of thin, stiff, sharp-pointed leaves and a large cluster of white flowers.

A perennial plant believed to be native to central and southern Mexico, though it is no longer found wild. It grows from underground tubers or tuberous roots and produces strongly fragrant, waxy white flowers.
edibilityNote: The flowers are used in cooking in Indonesia.

summary: A thornless evergreen shrub or small tree native to Australia. Its branches and narrow leaves hang down, while its shiny black seeds carry a crimson appendage.
edibilityNote: The seeds are edible.

summary: A bushy evergreen perennial native from Southeast Asia to Australia. Cultivated forms are prized for exceptionally varied leaves combining colors such as green, cream, pink, red and dark purple, with patterns and shapes that differ widely.

Rhizomatous perennial native to South Africa, the large fortnight lily has long, rigid, sword-like green leaves. Its white flowers carry yellow and violet markings, bloom abundantly during summer, especially after rain, and last only a couple of days.
An evergreen tree native to Borneo, Java and Peninsular Malaysia. It has long, spirally arranged leaves and gray to reddish bark marked with small horizontal flecks.

A bulbous herbaceous perennial native to Mexico, four-leaved wood-sorrel has four-part leaves and is widely grown as an ornamental. Its flowers and leaves are edible with a sharp lemon flavour, but eating too much can be harmful because its oxalic acid can interfere with nutrient absorption, especially calcium.
edibilityNote: Flowers and leaves are edible and lemon-flavoured, but excessive consumption can be harmful because oxalic acid may interfere with nutrient absorption, especially calcium.

summary: A wild banana species native to eastern South Asia, the eastern Indian subcontinent, northern Southeast Asia and southern China. Its lush leaves form upright clumps, and it has red to maroon flowers and blue-green fruit containing seeds.
edibilityNote: Natural clones, including wild saba bananas, produce edible fruit; seeded fruit is considered inedible, while historical cooking and eating of wild bananas is only assumed.

summary: A terrestrial orchid native to Costa Rica, Nicaragua, Panama, Colombia, Ecuador, Venezuela, Peru and Bolivia.

A unicellular green microalga found worldwide in freshwater and terrestrial habitats, it has spherical cells with a pea-green, cup-shaped chloroplast. Since the 1990s it has been considered a protein-rich food source and is now sold internationally as a dietary supplement or food additive.
edibilityNote: Since the 1990s, it has been used internationally as a dietary supplement or protein-rich food additive, including powders, tablets, capsules and extracts.

summary: A perennial flowering plant native to central and southern Europe, from Ireland, Britain and Portugal east to Turkey, Ukraine and the Baltic states. It is strongly aromatic, with hairy stems and one-sided clusters of usually white or pale pink flowers marked by a pinkish-purple blotch. It commonly grows in shady deciduous woodland.

summary: A biennial herb native to the Azores, Canaries, Madeira, North Africa, southern and eastern Europe, Switzerland, Mediterranean islands, western Asia and the Caucasus. It forms a soft, hairy leaf rosette in its first year, then flowers in its second. The flowers change from pink to pale blue with dark veins, while the fruits bear hooked spines.

summary: Woody-stemmed trailing perennial native to Italy and North Africa. Its light blue to violet flowers often have paler centres, and its stems do not twine.

A fast-growing tree native to the Indian subcontinent and parts of mainland Southeast Asia, neem is evergreen but sheds many leaves during dry winters. It has fragrant white flowers and smooth, olive-like fruits containing bitter-sweet, fibrous pulp.
edibilityNote: Tender shoots and flowers are eaten as vegetables in India; young leaves and flower buds are cooked or pickled in Southeast Asia. Neem oil is toxic to small children.

summary: A flowering plant native to western Peru, small-flowered tobacco has also been introduced to the Canary Islands. It is a parent of Nicotiana rustica, the economically important Aztec tobacco.

A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. There it grows in tall-herb meadows, woodland edges, farmland, olive groves and clearings, favoring cool, shady, organic-rich sites and generally limestone ground.

A deciduous tree native to Southern Europe and Southwestern Asia, manna ash retains smooth, dark-grey bark even when old. Dense clusters of slender, creamy-white flowers appear after the new leaves in late spring.

Small shrub-like succulent native to the Western Cape of South Africa. Its overlapping leaves grow in four rows, while vivid red flowers crowd into flat-topped clusters from December to March in its native habitat.

A biennial herb native to southwestern Europe. It has deeply divided green leaves and yellow, cross-shaped flowers, and often grows on river gravel, rocky slopes and disturbed ground. In Hungary, its seeds are used as seasoning.
edibilityNote: In Hungary, the seeds are used as seasoning.

summary: An annual herb native to the Mediterranean Basin of southern Europe, North Africa and western Asia. It is self-supporting, with broad compound leaves, and occurs in the North African Mediterranean–Sahara transition zone and human-altered landscapes.

A European perennial herb of wet places, with creeping stems that root at their joints. Its flowers are usually blue, occasionally white, and it grows beside water or in wet grassland, bogs and marshes.
A bulb-forming perennial of Europe and the Mediterranean, Meadow Gagea has generally yellow flowers, sometimes striped green on the back.

summary: A plant from North Africa and the Iberian Peninsula. Its leaflike stem expansions lack terminal spines and bear clusters of small flowers near their middle; the fruit is a vivid red berry. It grows in shady, damp places.

summary: A flowering plant species with no species-wide native origin supplied. In Portugal, its subspecies chium is native to the mainland and Madeira, while subspecies littoreum is native to the mainland.

A subshrub found in the western Mediterranean, including France, Portugal and Spain. Its stems and leathery leaves are densely hairy, especially beneath, while its yellow flowers have a hooded upper lip. It grows in dry grassland and scrub, particularly on limestone.

sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: Evergreen or semi-evergreen fern native to southern and western Europe. Its bright green, soft-textured fronds usually droop downslope, while cinnamon-brown scales coat the stalks and most midribs.

A low-growing plant of dry limestone rocks, occurring in parts of Europe, North Africa and the eastern Mediterranean. Its small leaves are green above but densely hairy and grey below, and its yellow flowers have five petals.

Evergreen shrub native near the southern coast of South Africa’s Western Cape. Its yellow, orange, or crimson flower heads resemble pincushions because their long styles project outward and curve upward; it flowers mainly from mid-July through November.

An evergreen succulent shrub native to Madagascar. Its olive-green, angular leaves become woolly near their tips and have darker tooth tips; it can reproduce through seeds and plantlets. It is naturally toxic to humans and may irritate exposed skin.
edibilityNote: Naturally toxic to humans; exposed skin may become irritated and itchy.

summary: A branching cactus probably native to the Peruvian Andes. Its stems bear spiral rows of bumps, long greyish-white spines and distinctive awl-shaped rudimentary leaves. It has become invasive in parts of the Mediterranean region and Australia.

A stem succulent native to Madagascar. Its silvery trunk bears large thorns and does most of the photosynthesis, while narrow leaves cluster at the top; outdoor plants develop large, fragrant white flowers but indoor plants rarely bloom.

A heath native to South Africa, Lesotho and Eswatini. Its form, hairiness and flowers vary markedly across its range, including a white-flowered form in Eswatini and Mpumalanga; it can resprout from its woody base after fire.
A flowering cactus native to Colombia, Ecuador and Peru, cane cactus is widely grown as an ornamental. It has become invasive in Europe, South Africa and Australia.
A small tree native to South Africa, with opposite branches and oval, pointed leaves that are hairy underneath. Its flowers are deep red.

A semi-evergreen shrub native to South Africa. Its narrow pink tubular flowers have crimson lobes and yellow throats, arranged in a single plane along one side of the stem. It flowers throughout summer but may behave as a perennial in cooler areas.

Perennial flowering plant native from Europe to the western Transcaucasus and northwestern Africa. It sprawls across damp woodland floors, rooting where its softly hairy stems touch moist soil, and bears small lilac flowers from late spring to early summer.

A large, upright columnar cactus from South America, the Venezuelan apple cactus has grey-green to blue stems with variable spines that may be absent. Its large cream flowers open for one night, and its thornless fruits contain sweetening white flesh and crunchy edible seeds.
edibilityNote: The thornless fruit has edible white flesh and small crunchy seeds; the flesh sweetens when the fruit opens fully.

summary: An evergreen shrub or small tree from Bhutan, China, India, Myanmar, Nepal, Pakistan, Sri Lanka and Thailand, it produces showy red, pink or white bell-shaped flowers in early to mid-spring. Its broad, dark green leaves have a silvery, fawn or brown hairy coating underneath.

A moss with green, bluish-green or occasionally yellowish growth and toothed leaves that curl when dry but spread when moist. Its distinctive spherical capsules begin green, then become brown and ridged with age.
A corm-growing plant endemic to the Western Cape, it occurs from Piketberg and the upper Olifants River Valley to the Kleinrivier and Riviersonderend Mountains as part of the fynbos.

An annual flowering plant occurring in Portugal. It grows in rock cracks, walls, roofs and sandy places regardless of substrate; reports that its petals are extensively joined into a tube require confirmation.
A biennial herb endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. The entire pale grey-green plant, including its fruit, is densely covered in soft, star-shaped hairs, while yellow flowers form a long, dense spike.

Herbaceous perennial native to the south-eastern Alps and the Balkans. Its five-lobed leaves are aromatic when crushed, and pale pink flowers appear in summer. Cultivated varieties range from white through pink to magenta.

Tender perennial herb native to humid, wet parts of Brazil and Paraguay. Its elongated leaves contain intensely sweet compounds; Guaraní people used the plant for centuries to sweeten yerba mate and as a treat, while processed leaf extracts serve as sugar substitutes.
edibilityNote: Guaraní people historically used the plant to sweeten yerba mate and as a treat; processed leaf extracts are used as sugar substitutes.

summary: A flowering shrub endemic to the Betic–Rif region, occurring in Andalusia and North Africa’s Tingitana Peninsula. Its square branches are densely woolly, its rough leaves are green above and whitish beneath, and its purple flowers have a hooded upper lip. It grows in scrub and open woodland on clay, marl or gypsum.

sources.title: Phlomis purpurea L.
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A herb endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. It has upright, ash-green stems that are usually hairy and slightly sticky, topped in spring and summer by yellow, two-lipped flowers with short spurs. It commonly occupies rocky cracks and dry, stony or sandy siliceous ground.

An annual herb endemic to central and western parts of the Iberian Peninsula. It bears one or more terminal flower heads with pale-yellow flowers and smaller brownish inner flowers. Its ribbed fruits lack both a beak and a feathery tuft.

Shrub or small tree native and widespread in New South Wales and Victoria; one subspecies is thought native in northern Tasmania but naturalised in the south. It has widely spreading, sharp needle-like leaves and warted woody fruit ending in a prominent beak with two small horns.
An annual clover distributed in Central and Western Europe, it has slightly drooping heads of five to seven bright yellowish-orange flowers from May to July. Its pods all turn in one direction.

A climbing or scrambling flowering plant endemic to eastern Australia. It has yellow flowers with more than thirty stamens, and their smell has been variously reported as resembling mothballs, animal urine or faeces.

An erect shrub endemic to eastern Australia, it has narrow leaves, shaggy young stems and crowded white flowers. Fire kills the plant, but it regenerates from seed and can also colonise sunny, unburnt sites.

A spreading shrub endemic to eastern Australia. It bears many mainly white flowers for several months from July, while its needle-shaped leaves end in sharp points and its rough fruits have a network of veins. Outside Australia it is invasive in South Africa, New Zealand and Portugal.

An upright shrub endemic to central eastern New South Wales, especially associated with sandstone country around Sydney. It has thin, firm bark, broad pointed leaves, relatively large white or pink flowers, and mature fruit that remains on the plant.
A small herbaceous perennial native to Australia. It has usually pale flowers and distinctive semicircular leaves that are dark green above and paler beneath.
An erect woody shrub endemic to eastern Australia. It has sharp-smelling leaves and dense heads of small white or pinkish flowers, which are widely used in floral arrangements.

A small, shrubby willow with a Eurosiberian Boreo-temperate range, it is widespread around western and northern European coasts. Its highly variable forms range, at least in the UK, from low, creeping, hairless plants to upright shrubs with silky leaves, occupying dunes, heaths, moors and fens.

summary: A water lily native to southern and eastern Asia, it blooms by day and has partly submerged or floating round leaves. Its flowers are usually white or blue, with angular petals creating a star-like shape.
edibilityNote: Rhizomes require boiling to neutralise toxins and have been eaten as famine food or medicine; cooked stems are also consumed as a vegetable in Bangladesh.

summary: A perennial plant found in southwestern Europe and North Africa. It is hairy and glandular throughout, sometimes slightly sticky, with fleshy leaves and white or pink flowers that often have a reddish central vein. It grows on rocky, base-poor ground, including cliffs, scree and walls.

summary: An annual herb native to mainland Portugal and recorded across the western Mediterranean, though records from Algeria and Morocco are uncertain. It is often branched at the base, with stiff spreading hairs and solitary blue, white and yellow flowers.

sources.title: Convolvulus meonanthus Hoffmanns. & Link
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A rhizomatous perennial iris native to temperate and tropical Asia, fringed iris spreads by wiry runners into dense carpets. Its pale blue, lavender or white flowers have fringed petals and a yellow or orange crest.
edibilityNote: In Japan, ground rhizomes provide starch; however, rhizomes and leaves are poisonous if mistakenly ingested and can cause stomach pain and vomiting.

summary: A low evergreen subshrub native to most of Europe and North Africa, with another passage also placing its native range in Asia. It forms creeping mats and strongly scented lilac, pink-purple or magenta flower clusters. It can be used like domestic thyme as a milder-flavoured herb.
edibilityNote: Used as an herb like domestic thyme, but with a milder flavour.

summary: Deciduous to semi-evergreen oak tree native to southern Portugal, Spain, Tunisia, Algeria and Morocco. It has shallow-lobed leaves and bears acorns in shallow cups. A 2016–2019 mainland Portuguese assessment classified its single national population as Critically Endangered, with fewer than 250 mature trees estimated around Serra de Monchique.

sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

summary: A houseplant species native to Brazil’s Atlantic Forest, the zebra-plant is sensitive to both too much and too little water. Its yellow bracts can persist for weeks, although the flowers last only a few days; the widely grown ‘Dania’ variety has deep green leaves with prominent white veins.

A succulent shrub originating from Central Africa, African milk tree is known only in cultivation. Its upright, two- or three-sided dark-green stems have pale V-shaped markings, paired thorns and drop-shaped leaves. It has never been known to flower and may be a hybrid; its poisonous latex can irritate skin.

An epiphytic orchid occurring from Trinidad and French Guiana through Venezuela and Colombia to northern Brazil. It has upright leafy stems and crowded, successively opening flowers that may be lavender, red, orange or yellow.

An evergreen flowering perennial native to tropical and southern Africa, the spider plant has long narrow leaves and fleshy, tuberous roots. Its arching flowering stems carry plantlets that droop, touch soil and form roots. The roots are reportedly edible, although preparation is unstated and mild laxative effects are claimed.
edibilityNote: Tuberous roots are reportedly edible, with raw or cooked preparation unstated; Nguni people claim mild laxative effects.

summary: Perennial fern native to Asia, extending from Southeast Asia to China, Japan, India, Sri Lanka, Pacific islands and Australia. Known as the Asian sword fern, it can grow up to 3 feet tall and has been introduced to the Americas and Hawaii.

A perennial flowering plant native to southwestern Europe and North Africa, it grows in somewhat moist meadows in Portugal’s Algarve under moderate grazing. There it has often been confused with another buttercup, so population estimates may be low.
